name: Achaemenid Persian army

weightNotes.aggression: Strategically offensive under Cyrus, Cambyses (Pelusium 525), Darius I (Scythia 513, Marathon 490) and Xerxes (480), but Darius III waited on prepared ground (Gaugamela, ground levelled for chariots). Mid value.
weightNotes.maneuver: Massive, slow multinational hosts; manoeuvre came from cavalry, not the army as a whole (Sekunda, Persian Army).
weightNotes.flanking: Cavalry was the striking arm and was used to envelop and raid: Plataea, cavalry raids blocked the Gargaphian spring and cut Greek supply; Gaugamela, wing cavalry tried to ride round the Macedonian right.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Competent besiegers (Ionian revolt sieges, Babylon), yet campaigns sought a decisive field battle with the king present. Below 0.5.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Deployed in one broad line by contingent with the Immortals around the king; little evidence of a held-back reserve committed deliberately.
weightNotes.scouting: Large cavalry arm and the royal road courier system gave reach, but Greek sources record repeated surprises; middling. Grade C because nearly all narrative is Greek.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Armies collapsed when the commander fell or fled (Plataea after Mardonius was killed, Issus and Gaugamela after Darius III fled), well before heavy losses; levy contingents had little cohesion.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Sparabara spearmen-archers behind wicker shields, cavalry, chariots, Greek mercenary hoplites and dozens of national contingents; arms existed but contingents fought by nation and were loosely integrated.
weightNotes.initiative: Command was centred on the king or a single royal commander; the army's fate followed his person (Cunaxa, Issus, Gaugamela). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Xerxes's 480 invasion was prepared for years with depots, the Athos canal and Hellespont bridges (Briant); fleet-supported advance along the coast. Scythia 513 shows the limit when the enemy stripped the land.

summary: An imperial army built on a Persian and Median core (the 10,000 Immortals, noble cavalry, sparabara archer-spearmen) and large levies of subject nations, later stiffened with Greek mercenary hoplites. It fought by first shooting: massed archery from behind a wicker shield wall, with cavalry using bow and javelin to harass, envelop and cut supply. It advanced with fleet support and prepared depots, and when on the defensive chose and prepared the battlefield.
whyItWorked: Scale, cavalry and archery overwhelmed Near Eastern states (Lydia, Babylon, Egypt at Pelusium) whose armies fought in the same idiom. Administrative reach let it mass and feed armies no rival could match, and competent siege work took Ionian and Cypriot cities.
whereItFailed: Against heavy close-order infantry that closed the distance: Marathon (490), Plataea (479), where the Spartan and Tegean hoplites broke through the shield wall and the army dissolved once Mardonius was killed. Against Macedonian combined arms: Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela (331), where Alexander's cavalry exploited a gap toward Darius. Against nomads who would not fight: Scythia (513), where scorched earth and blocked wells forced Darius to withdraw.

Scythian campaign of Darius I, Wikipedia
Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002), chapters on the royal army

name: Archetype: Bronze Age chariot states

weightNotes.aggression: Annual royal campaigning seasons into the Levant (Thutmose III's campaigns, Ramesses II at Kadesh); kings sought battle and tribute.
weightNotes.maneuver: Chariot mobility on open ground allowed fast strikes: at Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) Hittite chariotry crossed the river and hit the Egyptian Ra division on the march. Infantry-bound sieges pull it back to mid.
weightNotes.flanking: Chariot wings struck columns and flanks (Kadesh), but battle lines were simple; mid.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Campaigns aimed at city-states; Megiddo (15th c. BC) fell after a seven-month blockade with a moat and palisade rather than by assault. Field battle and blockade both common; just under mid.
weightNotes.reserveUse: At Kadesh Muwatalli II still held a large reserve of chariotry and infantry and sent another thousand chariots in a second wave; only partial evidence elsewhere.
weightNotes.scouting: Kadesh: Ramesses was misled by two captured nomads who were Hittite spies, and camped unaware of the enemy army behind Old Kadesh. Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Low-cohesion levy infantry and small elite chariot corps; armies broke quickly once the chariot arm was beaten. Educated guess anchored on ancient rout behaviour (Sabin 2000); grade C.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Chariots (archer platforms) with infantry runners and spearmen; Drews argues chariots were the decisive arm and infantry auxiliary, so integration was limited.
weightNotes.initiative: Command centred on the king in his chariot; outcomes followed his person (Ramesses at Kadesh). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Egyptian campaigns used coastal harbours and requisitioned harvests (Megiddo); chariots needed fodder and repair, tying armies to supply. Mid.

summary: Palace states (New Kingdom Egypt, Hittites, Mitanni, Mycenaean and Levantine kingdoms) fielded expensive elite chariot corps, each vehicle carrying a driver and a composite-bow archer (Hittite chariots three men), supported by levied and professional infantry. Kings campaigned each season against city-states; battles were won by massed chariot archery and charges on open ground, and cities taken by blockade.
whyItWorked: The chariot gave a stable, fast archery platform that out-shot and out-ran infantry on open ground, and only palace economies could afford horses, bows and specialist crews, so chariot states dominated their regions for centuries.
whereItFailed: Poor intelligence and march security: Kadesh, where Ramesses II was surprised in camp. Chariots were costly, fragile and useless on broken ground or against walls (Megiddo needed seven months). In the Late Bronze Age collapse (c. 1200 BC) chariot states fell to raiders and infantry, which Drews attributes to massed skirmishing infantry defeating chariot armies.

sources.title: Battle of Megiddo (15th century BC), Wikipedia
Drews, The End of the Bronze Age (1993)
Spalinger, War in Ancient Egypt: The New Kingdom (2005)
Sabin, The Face of Roman Battle, JRS 90 (2000)

name: Archetype: Iron Age and classical infantry states

weightNotes.aggression: Seasonal raiding and invasion to force battle was the norm (Hanson for Greece; Italic and Celtic warfare such as the Allia 390s BC and Sentinum 295 BC); slightly above mid.
weightNotes.maneuver: Close-order or loose infantry lines meeting frontally; manoeuvre mostly at the wings. Attrition-leaning.
weightNotes.flanking: Cavalry or light troops on the wings sometimes turned a flank (Sentinum, Gallic and Samnite wings), but rarely as a designed plan; below mid.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Most such states lacked siege trains and took towns by blockade, storm or betrayal; open battle and ravaging preferred.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Single-line deployments were typical outside Rome's triplex acies; little reserve.
weightNotes.scouting: Small cavalry arms; ambushes and surprises are frequent in the record (Allia). Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Krentz (GRBS 1985): defeated classical armies typically lost 10-20% killed including pursuit, so the break came under 10%; Sabin (2000) finds the same pattern for Roman-era battles.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Infantry core with some cavalry, slingers and javelinmen, loosely coordinated; mid-low.
weightNotes.initiative: Citizen or tribal levies under a king, elected magistrate or chief; little drill below the top.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Short campaigns on rations and foraging near home; armies dispersed at harvest or when supplies ran out.

summary: Generic profile for Iron Age and classical states whose strength was infantry: Italic peoples, Celtic and Iberian tribes, smaller Greek and Hellenistic states and similar. Armies of citizen or tribal levies fought in a main infantry line with cavalry and skirmishers on the wings, in short summer campaigns of raiding and pitched battle. Battles were decided in hours by the collapse of one line, with most deaths in the pursuit.
whyItWorked: Cheap to raise from free farmers, effective at defending home territory, and able to field large numbers for a single decisive battle; heavy infantry was hard to stop frontally on level ground.
whereItFailed: Against professional, combined-arms or drilled enemies that could absorb shock and exploit flanks: Celtic and Samnite armies against Rome (Sentinum 295 BC), Greek states against Macedon (Chaeronea 338 BC), and against cavalry or horse-archer armies on open ground. Lack of siege craft and logistics prevented decisive wars of conquest.

sources.title: Krentz, Casualties in Hoplite Battles, GRBS 26 (1985)
Sabin, The Face of Roman Battle, JRS 90 (2000)
Hanson, The Western Way of War (2nd ed. 2000)

name: Archetype: Soviet-model armies (Warsaw Pact and clients, 1945-91)

weightNotes.aggression: FM 100-2-1 (1984): Soviet doctrine is offensive, aiming to seize the initiative at the outset of hostilities and carry the war onto enemy territory; defence is a temporary phase.
weightNotes.maneuver: Deep operation and the operational maneuver group (OMG) aim at tempo and depth (FM 100-2-1 ch. 4; CIA 1983 OMG assessment), but by massing on narrow breakthrough sectors with heavy artillery. A mix of mass and manoeuvre, so 0.6.
weightNotes.flanking: Doctrine prefers bypassing strongpoints, envelopment and exploitation into the rear by mobile groups and air assault; tactically, attacks still went in on norm-prescribed narrow frontages. Middling-high.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Cities are bypassed and left to second echelons; advance norms of up to about 30-50 km a day (FM 100-2-1) leave no time for sieges. Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: FM 100-2-1: second echelons were as much as half of an attacking formation (two divisions of a four-division army) when facing deep defences, plus combined-arms and special reserves; lighter when the defender was thin.
weightNotes.scouting: Dedicated reconnaissance units at every echelon, Spetsnaz and the reconnaissance-strike complex concept; middling because tactical intelligence fusion was slow and rigid.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Formations were expected to fight until exhausted and then be passed through by the next echelon rather than withdraw; high casualty acceptance. 0.3 kept below modern breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Combined arms combat is the core of Soviet doctrine (FM 100-2-1): tank, motor rifle, artillery, air defence, engineers and frontal aviation integrated by norm. Below the Western profile because coordination was rigid and pre-planned.
weightNotes.initiative: FM 100-2-1, 'Norms, initiative and flexibility': a given situation has an approved normative response; 'probably little tactical flexibility at subunit level (battalion and lower)'; flexibility grows with rank.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Norms prescribe supply rates and a push-forward system, but the offensive design accepts outrunning supply for the sake of tempo. Middling.

summary: Massive mechanised armies built on the Soviet model: tank and motor rifle divisions, very large artillery parks and integrated air defence, fighting by mathematical norms. The offensive seeks a breakthrough on a narrow sector with crushing artillery density (FM 100-2-1 cites 60-100 tubes per km on a main attack), followed by second echelons and operational maneuver groups exploiting deep into the enemy rear at high tempo. Command is centralised; junior commanders execute drills. Cadre divisions fill out by mass mobilisation of reservists.
whyItWorked: Mass, tempo and simplicity: norms and drills let a conscript army execute complex operations, and echeloning sustained the momentum of an offensive in a way NATO planners feared enough to rewrite their doctrine (AirLand Battle and Follow-on Forces Attack). It crushed Hungary 1956 and Czechoslovakia 1968 quickly and North Korea's 1950 offensive nearly overran the South.
whereItFailed: Afghanistan 1979-1989: a force designed for European mechanised war struggled against dispersed mujahideen in mountains and had to improvise with air assault and small-unit tactics (Grau, The Bear Went Over the Mountain). Client armies with Soviet kit and doctrine but less training were routed by Western-model forces: Egypt and Syria 1967 and 1973 (after the Canal crossing), Iraq 1991. Rigidity left units helpless when the plan broke.

Grau (ed.), The Bear Went Over the Mountain: Soviet Combat Tactics in Afghanistan (1998)

Pollack, Armies of Sand: The Past, Present, and Future of Arab Military Effectiveness (2019)

name: Archetype: NATO-model armies (1945-91), Active Defense to AirLand Battle

weightNotes.aggression: In Europe the posture was defensive (forward defence of West Germany; FM 100-5 1976 'Active Defense' was criticised for prioritising defence, TRADOC history). Elsewhere Western armies attacked: Inchon 1950, Falklands 1982, Desert Storm 1991. Average 0.5.
weightNotes.maneuver: 1976 Active Defense leaned on firepower and force ratios (TRADOC history); 1982/86 FM 100-5 shifted to manoeuvre with tenets initiative, depth, agility and synchronization. 0.65 averages the era, weighted to its end.
weightNotes.flanking: AirLand Battle sought to strike the enemy's flanks and rear and attack second echelons in depth; Inchon 1950 and the 1991 left hook are the canonical examples.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Doctrine aimed at the enemy's forces and follow-on echelons, not cities; urban fighting (Hue 1968) was incidental. Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: NATO corps sectors kept armoured counterattack reserves behind a covering force and main battle area; middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Armoured cavalry regiments, air reconnaissance, SIGINT and, late in the era, JSTARS and satellite imagery; better than Warsaw Pact ISR.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Active Defense explicitly traded space for time with units falling back between battle positions; democracies' casualty sensitivity after Vietnam. 0.2, below breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Tank-mechanised infantry-artillery teams with close air support; AirLand Battle formalised air-ground integration (FM 100-5 1982).
weightNotes.initiative: FM 100-5 1982: commanders 'must encourage initiative in their subordinates'; German Auftragstaktik heritage in the Bundeswehr and British mission command. Uneven across NATO armies, so 0.7.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Heavy, well-resourced logistics with prepositioned stocks (POMCUS) and REFORGER; Desert Storm paused for a large logistics build-up before the ground war. High.

summary: Professional or long-service conscript armies (US, UK, West Germany, France, Israel as a close cousin) built to defeat a numerically superior Warsaw Pact. From 1976 the US Active Defense fought from successive battle positions with superior anti-tank firepower, trading space for time; from 1982 AirLand Battle added deep attack on enemy second echelons, manoeuvre against flanks and rear, and tight air-ground integration. Outside Europe the same armies conducted amphibious landings, strategic bombing campaigns and limited wars.
whyItWorked: Quality over quantity: better training, junior leadership and technology (thermal sights, attack helicopters, precision munitions late in the era) and air superiority. Desert Storm 1991, the doctrine's only full test against a Soviet-equipped army, destroyed the Iraqi army in about 100 hours of ground war. Israel 1967 and 1973 (after the first days) show the same model beating Soviet-model forces.
whereItFailed: Vietnam 1965-73: a conventional, firepower-heavy approach could not defeat a political insurgency backed by a regular army (Krepinevich, The Army and Vietnam); attrition by body count failed. Korea 1950: unprepared US units were routed by the North Korean offensive and then surprised by Chinese intervention at the Chongchon and Chosin. Its central-front promise was never tested against the Warsaw Pact.

Krepinevich, The Army and Vietnam (Johns Hopkins, 1986)
Pollack, Armies of Sand (2019), on Arab-Israeli and Gulf wars

name: Archetype: medieval feudal host

weightNotes.aggression: Tactically impetuous (knights charging prematurely at Crecy 1346 and Nicopolis 1396), but strategically battle-averse: most campaigns were raids and sieges and pitched battles were rare (Verbruggen). The two average to mid.
weightNotes.maneuver: Armies moved slowly with baggage and fought frontal set pieces; chevauchee raiding was the main form of operational movement.
weightNotes.flanking: Mounted wings and occasional feigned flights (Normans at Hastings 1066, Arques, Messina, Cassel) show some flanking skill, but most battles were frontal charges.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Castles and walled towns dominated medieval warfare; sieges took months or years with engines and mining (Medieval warfare; Chateau Gaillard 1203-04). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Hosts deployed in three battles (vanguard, main, rear) and the rear often acted as a reserve (Verbruggen); usually committed piecemeal.
weightNotes.scouting: Reconnaissance was often neglected: the French at Courtrai (1302) charged over ditches dug and concealed by the Flemings; at Nicopolis the French knights refused to wait two hours for Sigismund's scouts to report on the Ottoman dispositions. Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Armoured knights could absorb more punishment than ancient infantry, but levies broke early; 0.1 sits below the low end of the breakpoint range. Educated guess, grade C.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Knights with crossbowmen, archers and foot, poorly integrated in most hosts: at Crecy the French cavalry rode through their own fleeing crossbowmen. English 14th-c. armies are the exception.
weightNotes.initiative: Command fragmented among lords whose chivalric code demanded the honour of the first charge (Nicopolis); decentralised but not mission tactics, and prone to uncontrolled pursuit.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Limited feudal service terms, foraging and pillage (chevauchee) instead of depots; hosts dispersed when pay or food ran out.

summary: Armies raised through feudal obligation and, increasingly, pay: mounted men-at-arms (knights) as the striking arm, supported by crossbowmen, archers and infantry levies, deployed in three battles. Most warfare was raiding (chevauchee) to destroy an opponent's revenue and sieges of castles and walled towns with trebuchets, towers and mines; pitched battles were rare and risky and usually decided by the knights' charge.
whyItWorked: The armoured mounted charge was decisive against unprepared foot on open ground, and the castle network made territory defensible by small garrisons. Siege skill was high: engines, mining and blockade could take strong fortresses such as Chateau Gaillard (1204).
whereItFailed: Undisciplined charges into prepared infantry and missile troops: Courtrai (1302) against Flemish militia behind ditches, Bannockburn (1314) against Scottish schiltrons, Crecy (1346) against English longbowmen, Nicopolis (1396) against the Ottomans. Against mobile horse-archer armies the knights were drawn into pursuit and destroyed: Hattin (1187), where Saladin cut the crusader army off from water.

sources.title: Battle of the Golden Spurs (Courtrai), Wikipedia
Verbruggen, The Art of Warfare in Western Europe during the Middle Ages (2nd ed. 1997)

name: Archetype: linear warfare armies (1600-1789)

weightNotes.aggression: Trained long-service soldiers were expensive and hard to replace, which was 'a major deterrent to battle' (warhistory.org, Prussian practice 1740-1763); generals often manoeuvred for months without fighting. Frederick II was the aggressive exception.
weightNotes.maneuver: Lines advanced very slowly, giving the enemy time to shift reserves; armies manoeuvred against each other's supply lines rather than seeking destruction (warhistory.org).
weightNotes.flanking: Cavalry on the wings tried to outflank the enemy; Frederick's oblique order (Leuthen 1757) refused one wing and attacked the other in echelon (warhistory.org). Most battles were still parallel-line firefights.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Fortress warfare dominated (Vauban's sieges, the Low Countries campaigns of the Spanish and Austrian Succession wars); campaigns were often decided by which fortresses fell. High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Standard order of battle was two lines about 200 m apart, the second acting as reserve to relieve the first or stop a cavalry breakthrough (warhistory.org). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Hussars and light troops screened and patrolled, mainly as security against desertion and raids (Frederick, General Principles of War); operational reconnaissance was patchy.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Beaten armies usually withdrew in good order because their formations were rarely broken, and pursuit was weak (warhistory.org). Low threshold: commanders broke off rather than lose irreplaceable men.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Infantry in the centre, cavalry on the wings, battalion guns between battalions: three arms on one field, but in rigid separate roles with little mutual support (warhistory.org).
weightNotes.initiative: Rigid drill and close supervision, partly to prevent desertion of soldiers 'tied to no bond' with the state (Frederick, General Principles of War). Very low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies lived from magazines (Louvois' system, about 15 days' reserve; Jelinek, DTIC AD1022125) and stayed within a few marches of them; Frederick judged wars far from one's borders 'useless'. High.

summary: Standing professional armies of long-service soldiers, many of them foreign or pressed, fought in long thin lines three ranks deep, infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings, trading volleys at close range. Drill gave fire discipline and kept men from deserting. Armies moved slowly, tied to magazines and bread ovens, and much of every war was fortress warfare: Vauban-style sieges and entrenched lines. Battles were costly and rarely decisive because beaten armies usually withdrew intact and pursuit was weak.
whyItWorked: Disciplined volley fire made the line the most effective way to use smoothbore muskets, and the magazine system let armies campaign without destroying the country they depended on. Limited war suited dynastic states with limited money and men. In the right hands (Frederick at Rossbach and Leuthen, 1757) the system could still deliver decisive victories.
whereItFailed: Battles were attritional and rarely ended wars (Malplaquet 1709, Zorndorf 1758, Kunersdorf 1759); pursuit was weak. Line troops fighting irregulars in broken terrain were cut up (Braddock at the Monongahela, 1755). Against mass conscript armies living off the land and fighting in columns and skirmish swarms, the system collapsed (Valmy and Jemappes 1792, Jena 1806).

sources.title: Military practice in Prussia 1740-1763: the tactical level (warhistory.org)
Frederick II, General Principles of War (1748/1753), German History in Documents and Images
Jelinek, Napoleon's Logistics (ACSC paper, DTIC AD1022125), section on the ancien-regime magazine system
House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 1 'Prologue to 1914'

name: Archetype: industrial mass conscript armies (1850-1918)

weightNotes.aggression: The pre-1914 'cult of the offensive' (Plan XVII, the Schlieffen plan) and repeated mass offensives on the Western Front 1915-17 despite losses (House ch. 1-2; Lupfer). Above middle.
weightNotes.maneuver: Railway mobilisation allowed operational manoeuvre (1866, 1870, Tannenberg 1914), but tactically the war became positional attrition once fronts closed in late 1914 (House ch. 2). Low.
weightNotes.flanking: Wide envelopments were the operational ideal (Sedan 1870, the 1914 Schlieffen wheel, Tannenberg) until continuous fronts removed open flanks. Moderate.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Fortress sieges recurred (Metz and Paris 1870, Plevna 1877, Port Arthur 1904, Liege and Verdun); Verdun 1916 was designed to bleed the enemy at a fortress he had to hold. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Mass reserve formations mobilised by rail, and from 1917 deliberate counterattack divisions held behind the front in the elastic defence (Lupfer). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Cavalry screens failed against magazine rifles; early aerial reconnaissance helped (Tannenberg, the Marne) but tactical intelligence of enemy depth stayed poor. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Attacks were pressed through very heavy losses (Somme, 1 July 1916; Verdun), yet armies could also withdraw in order (the 1914 retreat to the Marne, the 1917 Hindenburg Line withdrawal). Moderate-high. Judgment.
weightNotes.combinedArms: 1914 armies coordinated infantry and artillery poorly; by 1917-18 creeping barrages, infiltration tactics, tanks and ground-attack aircraft produced real all-arms battle (House ch. 2; Lupfer). Average across the period.
weightNotes.initiative: Centralised timetables and rigid fire plans; the German army's 1917-18 shift to decentralised stormtroop and defence-in-depth methods is the notable exception (Lupfer). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies were tied to railheads; offensives that outran them stalled (the Marne 1914, the 1918 German spring offensives). Moderate-high.

summary: Universal conscription and reserve systems produced armies of millions, mobilised and moved by railway and supplied by industrial economies. Before 1914 doctrine stressed the offensive and moral force; magazine rifles, machine guns and quick-firing artillery made frontal assault ruinously costly, and by late 1914 continuous trench lines from the Channel to Switzerland removed the flanks. The war became one of artillery and attrition, broken only by the slow development of infiltration tactics, elastic defence in depth, creeping barrages, tanks and air support in 1916-18.
whyItWorked: Mass and industry let a state absorb enormous losses and keep fighting for years; railways concentrated reserves faster than any attacker could exploit a breach, which made the defence dominant. Prussia's general staff system turned this into quick decisive wars in 1866 and 1870, and Germany's 1917 elastic defence in depth beat back the Nivelle and Passchendaele offensives (Lupfer).
whereItFailed: Frontal offensives against entrenched machine guns and artillery: the Battles of the Frontiers 1914, Gallipoli 1915, Verdun and the Somme 1916 (about 57,000 British casualties on the first day), the Nivelle offensive and the French mutinies of 1917, Passchendaele 1917. The German 1918 spring offensives broke through tactically but had no mobile exploitation force and outran their railheads.

sources.title: Lupfer, The Dynamics of Doctrine: The Changes in German Tactical Doctrine During the First World War (Leavenworth Paper 4, DTIC ADA563816)
House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 1-2

name: Archetype: guerrilla and insurgent forces

weightNotes.aggression: Mao, On Guerrilla Warfare: attack only where and when the enemy is weak and avoid battles that cannot be won; FM 3-24 (2006) describes protracted struggle designed to weaken government control rather than seek decisive battle. Low.
weightNotes.maneuver: Pure manoeuvre in the sense of avoiding attrition: disperse, strike, vanish (Jalali and Grau, The Other Side of the Mountain, on mujahideen raids and ambushes). High.
weightNotes.flanking: Ambushes on columns and lines of communication, attacks on flanks and rear rather than fronts; the dominant mujahideen and Viet Cong tactic. High.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Insurgents rarely hold or besiege cities; they operate from rural terrain (RAND How Insurgencies End: insurgencies suited to rural terrain). Exceptions (ISIS Mosul 2014-17) ended badly for the insurgent. Very low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Small bands commit what they have to a raid; the 'reserve' is the population and sanctuary, not a held-back force. Low.
weightNotes.scouting: FM 3-24: insurgents draw intelligence from the population they live among; local knowledge and informants see the counterinsurgent's moves. High, though without technical ISR.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Doctrine is to break contact early and preserve the force (Mao's sixteen-character formula opens 'the enemy advances, we retreat'). Lowest of all profiles; well below breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Light infantry with small arms, RPGs, mortars, IEDs; no armour or air. Very low.
weightNotes.initiative: Cells and bands act on local judgement under loose political direction; decentralisation is forced by dispersion (Jalali and Grau). High, though coordination between groups is poor.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: RAND How Insurgencies End: 'sanctuary is vital to insurgents' and withdrawal of state sponsorship typically leads to defeat; operations stay near base areas, caches and borders. Middling-high.

summary: Irregular forces fighting a protracted war against a stronger state or occupier: Viet Cong, Afghan mujahideen, Iraqi insurgents 2003-11, the Taliban, many African and Latin American movements. They avoid pitched battle, disperse among the population, ambush convoys and patrols, use IEDs, raids and terrorism, and fall back to rural or cross-border sanctuaries. Mao's three phases (strategic defence, stalemate, counteroffensive) describe the ideal path from guerrilla war to regular war.
whyItWorked: Protracted conflict favours the insurgent (FM 3-24): the stronger side cannot find a decisive target and its political will erodes. RAND's study of 89 insurgencies finds they last about ten years on average. Mujahideen with outside sponsorship and Pakistani sanctuary forced the Soviet withdrawal in 1989; Iraqi insurgents and the Taliban outlasted the US (Iraq 2011, Afghanistan 2021).
whereItFailed: When sanctuary and sponsorship are removed or the insurgent tries to hold ground: RAND finds withdrawal of state sponsorship typically leads to defeat and terrorism often backfires. ISIS lost its cities (Mosul, Raqqa 2017) once it fought conventionally; the Tamil Tigers were destroyed in 2009 after shifting to conventional defence; the Viet Cong were gutted in the 1968 Tet Offensive when they massed in the open.

sources.title: Mao Tse-tung, On Guerrilla Warfare (1937), Marxists Internet Archive
Connable and Libicki, How Insurgencies End (RAND MG-965, 2010)
Jalali and Grau, The Other Side of the Mountain: Mujahideen Tactics in the Soviet-Afghan War, Internet Archive
Rayburn and Sobchak, The U.S. Army in the Iraq War, Vol. 1 (US Army War College Press, 2019)

name: Archetype: regional middle powers with mixed Soviet/Western equipment

weightNotes.aggression: Mixed record: Iraq 1990 (Kuwait), Ethiopia-Eritrea 1998-2000, Azerbaijan 2020 and 2023, Saudi-led Yemen 2015- all show willingness to start wars over regional disputes; others mostly deter. Middle value.
weightNotes.maneuver: Pollack (Armies of Sand) documents set-piece, top-down operations with little exploitation; Iran-Iraq and Ethiopia-Eritrea became trench wars. Azerbaijan 2020 is the exception that moved fast with drones and special forces.
weightNotes.flanking: Mostly frontal, pre-planned attacks along roads; few operational envelopments outside Azerbaijan 2020 (mountain infiltration to Shusha). Low-middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Regional wars are fought over territory and towns (Basra and Khorramshahr in the Iran-Iraq War, Badme, Shusha, Saada); objective scoring weights cities more than Western profiles.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Regime-protection units (Republican Guard type) are held back from the front as a political reserve; middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Generally weak tactical intelligence (Pollack); Azerbaijan 2020 showed what a drone-rich regional force can do (CSIS: TB2 and loitering munitions found and destroyed T-72s and S-300s). Average 0.4.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Conscript-heavy, politicised armies tend to break rather than withdraw in good order (Iraq 1991, Pollack), so the good-order threshold is low and the morale breakpoint does the rest. Educated guess.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Pollack's central finding on Arab militaries: poor integration of armour, infantry, artillery and air at tactical level, despite good equipment; mixed Soviet/Western kit complicates logistics and C2.
weightNotes.initiative: Pollack: over-centralisation, lack of tactical initiative and information-hoarding by junior officers, rooted in politicised command and culture; generalised here to the archetype.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Supply systems that work in static warfare but break during deep advances (Iraq in Iran 1980, Saudi coalition in Yemen). Middling.

summary: Middle powers such as Iraq, Iran, Egypt, Syria, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, fielding mixed Soviet/Russian, Western, Chinese, Turkish and Israeli equipment. They fight top-down, artillery-heavy, set-piece battles over contested territory and towns, often settling into fortified fronts. Better-funded states now add drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles that can be decisive against peers lacking air defence.
whyItWorked: Against similar opponents, firepower, numbers and fortification decide: Iraq held off Iran for eight years from fortified lines with massed artillery. Azerbaijan 2020 won the 44-day Nagorno-Karabakh war by pairing oil-funded drones and precision missiles (Israeli LORA, Turkish TB2, Harop) with ground offensives against an Armenian army with legacy Soviet systems (CSIS).
whereItFailed: Against Western-model forces they are routed: Iraq 1991 and 2003. Pollack attributes Arab armies' poor showing to tactical leadership, initiative and combined arms, not equipment. Armenia 2020 showed a Soviet-model army without counter-drone defence losing tanks and S-300s to cheap UAVs. Iran-Iraq and Ethiopia-Eritrea attrition produced huge casualties for little territorial change.

sources.title: CSIS, The Air and Missile War in Nagorno-Karabakh: Lessons for the Future of Strike and Defense (2020)
Pollack, Armies of Sand: The Past, Present, and Future of Arab Military Effectiveness (Oxford UP, 2019)
RUSI, Preliminary Lessons in Conventional Warfighting from Russia's Invasion of Ukraine (on UAS and counter-UAS)

name: Archetype: small modern militaries, territorial and total defence

weightNotes.aggression: Doctrine is to deter, delay and hold until allies arrive (RAND RR-2779 on Baltic total defence: 'buy time for' national and NATO conventional responses). Counterattacks only locally.
weightNotes.maneuver: Small mechanised cores (often one or two brigades) plus large territorial forces; defence-oriented positional fighting with local mobile counterattacks. Below middle.
weightNotes.flanking: Home-terrain knowledge favours ambush and raids on enemy flanks and columns (Ukrainian territorial units north of Kyiv, 2022), but formations are too small for operational envelopment.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Defends its own cities rather than seeking enemy ones; objective scoring should favour own threatened cities. Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Mobilised reservists and national guard (Estonian Defence League, Latvian national guard, RAND RR-2779) form a sizeable second line; middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Excellent local knowledge, civilian reporting networks and cheap drones; limited strategic ISR without allies. Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Delay doctrine trades space for time and preserves forces for resistance; RAND's Baltic wargames showed conventional defence collapsing within 60 hours, so withdrawing early to cities and forests is the plan. 0.2.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Modern but thin: anti-tank missiles, mortars, some artillery and air defence; little or no air force. Middling.
weightNotes.initiative: Small professional cadres and reservists trained for decentralised resistance (RAND RR-2779 on unconventional warfare and resistance); Nordic and Baltic forces use mission command. Educated judgement.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Fights on interior lines inside its own supply network with prepositioned caches; operations rarely leave home territory. High.

summary: Small states (Baltic and Nordic states, Switzerland, Singapore-style conscript forces, Georgia, Taiwan in its newer concepts) that cannot match a great-power neighbour. They combine a small professional or conscript core with mass reservists, territorial defence units and whole-of-society 'total defence': delay on prepared positions and obstacles, fight from cities and forests, keep resistance going behind enemy lines, and hold long enough for allies to intervene.
whyItWorked: Raises the cost and time of invasion: RAND RR-2779 finds total defence and unconventional warfare improve warning, augment initial defences and buy time for NATO. Ukraine 2022 showed a defender that dispersed its forces and used massed fires from two artillery brigades blunting a force with a 12:1 local advantage on the approaches to Kyiv (RUSI Preliminary Lessons).
whereItFailed: Alone, against a major power, it cannot hold territory: RAND's 2014-15 wargames had Russian forces reach the outskirts of Tallinn and/or Riga within 60 hours at most (RR-1253), and RAND RR-2779 frames total defence as a complement to conventional national and NATO defence, not a substitute for it. Georgia 2008 lost its conventional battle within five days.

sources.title: RAND, Deterring Russian Aggression in the Baltic States Through Resilience and Resistance (RR-2779)
RAND, Reinforcing Deterrence on NATO's Eastern Flank: Wargaming the Defense of the Baltics (RR-1253)
RUSI, Preliminary Lessons in Conventional Warfighting from Russia's Invasion of Ukraine: February-July 2022

name: Archetype: steppe nomad confederations

weightNotes.aggression: Constant raiding of settled neighbours, but set battles were avoided unless the odds were good (Scythians against Darius 513 BC refused battle). Mid.
weightNotes.maneuver: Wholly mounted armies with remount herds; mobility was the whole system (Mounted archery; Hildinger, Warriors of the Steppe).
weightNotes.flanking: Envelopment by horse archers and the feigned flight into an ambush were standard (Parthian shot, Scythian and Hunnic practice).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Before the Mongols most confederations could not take walled cities except by surprise, starvation or hired engineers (Huns at Orleans 451 failed to finish the siege). Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Bands dispersed to harass and regrouped; some held a lancer reserve, mostly not.
weightNotes.scouting: Steppe life made every rider a scout and wide screens were normal; below the Mongol 0.95 because intelligence networks were less systematic.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Nomad units broke contact early by design and returned later; avoiding attrition was the doctrine. Lowest of all profiles.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Horse archers dominant with some noble heavy lancers; no infantry or siege arm worth the name in most cases.
weightNotes.initiative: Clan and tribal bands acting under their own chiefs within a loose confederation: decentralised, but also poorly coordinated, so mid.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies lived on herds and plunder and raided far beyond any supply network; campaigns were seasonal and limited by grass. Low strictness.

summary: Pastoral confederations (Scythians, Xiongnu, Huns, Avars, Magyars, Cumans and later Turkic and Mongol successors) fought as mounted archers with several horses per man. They raided settled states, avoided battle on bad terms, harassed with arrows, feigned flight to break the enemy's formation and finished with lancers. When invaded they retreated into the steppe, stripping pasture and blocking wells until the invader starved.
whyItWorked: Settled armies could not catch them or bring them to battle, and their bows out-ranged infantry on open ground. The steppe itself was a defence: no city to capture, and an invader's supply could not follow. Darius I's Scythian campaign (513 BC) ended in withdrawal against scorched earth and refusal of battle.
whereItFailed: When a settled state built its own cavalry and logistics and pushed into the steppe: Mobei (119 BC), where Han armies under Wei Qing and Huo Qubing defeated the Xiongnu. When forced to fight heavy troops on ground they could not leave or after plunder slowed them: Lechfeld (955) for the Magyars. Against walls and combined Roman-Germanic coalitions: the Catalaunian Plains (451) and Orleans for the Huns. Confederations also broke up on a leader's death.

sources.title: Scythian campaign of Darius I, Wikipedia
Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, Wikipedia

name: Archetype: infantry armies with limited mechanisation (1914-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: Mostly defensive postures by smaller states facing larger industrial neighbours (Poland 1939, Yugoslavia and Greece 1941, China 1937-45), with local offensives. Middle-low.
weightNotes.maneuver: Foot infantry and horse-drawn artillery move at marching pace; mechanised formations were absent or a handful of brigades (House ch. 3-4). Low.
weightNotes.flanking: Horse cavalry and light infantry could still envelop in forests and broken terrain (Finnish motti tactics at Suomussalmi 1939-40) but not against motorised enemies. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Defended cities, fortified lines and border regions for political and economic reasons (Poland covered the Corridor, Poznan and Silesian industry; DA Pam 20-255 part one). Moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Cordon deployments along long frontiers left thin reserves that could not reach a breach in time (Poland 1939; House ch. 4). Low-moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Horse cavalry, few aircraft and scarce radios; the German attack was a tactical surprise to the Polish army despite known concentrations (DA Pam 20-255 ch. 6). Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Withdrawal in good order at moderate losses where roads allowed; foot armies were often encircled before they could disengage. Judgment.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Few tanks, little antitank capacity, scarce radios and almost no close air support (House ch. 3-4); artillery-infantry cooperation at First World War standard.
weightNotes.initiative: Mostly centralised command on the First World War model; varies by army (Finnish small-unit initiative was high). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Rail- and horse-bound supply kept operations close to railheads; consumption was low, so foot armies could keep going on short rations. Middle.

summary: Conscript infantry armies of 1914-1945 that lacked the industry for large-scale mechanisation: rifle divisions marching on foot, artillery and supply drawn by horses, horse cavalry for reconnaissance, a few tank battalions and a small air force. They fought on First World War lines: entrenched linear defence along frontiers or rivers, deliberate infantry-artillery attacks, and withdrawal by rail and road. Examples: the Polish army of 1939, the Yugoslav, Greek and Romanian armies, the Chinese National Revolutionary Army, and the Finnish army of the Winter War.
whyItWorked: On terrain that denied mechanised forces (forest, mountains, marsh, winter) and against road-bound enemies, cheap infantry held well and could even win: Finnish motti encirclements at Suomussalmi (1939-40), Greek mountain fighting against Italy (1940-41), Chinese defence and the Taierzhuang victory (1938). Low consumption made these armies durable on poor logistics.
whereItFailed: Against mechanised, air-supported opponents in open country they were outmanoeuvred and encircled: Poland 1939 (cordon defence on the frontier, broken in days; DA Pam 20-255), Yugoslavia in eleven days and Greece in April 1941, Shanghai and Nanjing 1937, and the Romanian Third and Fourth Armies at Stalingrad in November 1942, which lacked antitank guns to stop Soviet tank corps.

sources.title: House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 3-4
Kennedy, The German Campaign in Poland (1939), DA Pamphlet 20-255
Lupfer, The Dynamics of Doctrine (Leavenworth Paper 4, DTIC ADA563816)

name: British Army, RAF and Royal Navy doctrine (1939-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: Two phases: 1940-42 frequent offensives pushed by London before units were trained (House ch. 4, desert war); 1942-45 Montgomery's cautious 'Colossal Cracks' set-pieces launched only with overwhelming material (Hart). Middle value.
weightNotes.maneuver: 1942-45 doctrine was firepower-heavy attrition to conserve scarce infantry (Hart, Colossal Cracks). 1940 Compass and some desert operations were genuinely mobile, which keeps it above the French value.
weightNotes.flanking: Compass 1940 hooked round the Italian camps and cut the coast road at Beda Fomm (House ch. 4); Market Garden 1944 tried to outflank the Westwall. Most 1942-45 attacks (Alamein, Caen, Goodwood) were frontal break-ins.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Defended key ports and cities (Tobruk 1941, Malta) and fought for Caen as a named objective; offensives generally targeted enemy formations through set-piece battles.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Montgomery insisted on 'balance', always keeping a reserve to meet counterattacks (X Corps at Alamein); House ch. 4 describes defence as blocking positions in depth plus massive counterattacks.
weightNotes.scouting: Ultra signals intelligence, RAF photographic reconnaissance and the RN's intelligence centre gave the best strategic intelligence of the war, although tactical recon in 1940-42 was weak. High.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Britain's manpower shortage made casualty conservation central from 1943 (Hart); attacks were halted rather than pressed at heavy cost. Low.
weightNotes.combinedArms: 1940-42 armour charged antitank gun lines without infantry and artillery (Battleaxe, 15 June 1941; House ch. 4). 1942-45 artillery-infantry integration became very good (Parham's mass-fire method). Average of the two phases.
weightNotes.initiative: Montgomery held that deliberate attack and defence must be 'stage-managed' at the highest level with centralised control (House ch. 4); subordinate initiative was limited outside fluid pursuit.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Large build-ups before every offensive (Alamein, Normandy) and reluctance to advance beyond supply; Market Garden is the main exception. High.

summary: A small, volunteer-based professional army expanded by conscription, backed by the world's largest navy and an independent air force committed to strategic bombing. After defeats in 1940-42, the army settled on Montgomery's method: build up overwhelming artillery, armour and supplies, then fight a centrally controlled set-piece battle that wore the enemy down with firepower while saving British infantry, followed by limited exploitation. The Royal Artillery's quick mass-fire procedures let a single observer bring whole regiments onto a target. Sea power, the blockade and joint amphibious landings carried the war to the enemy; RAF Bomber Command waged a night area-bombing campaign against German industry and cities.
whyItWorked: Firepower and logistics played to British strengths (industry, sea lanes, US and Commonwealth supply) and protected scarce manpower. Ultra intelligence let commanders fight on known enemy dispositions (Alam Halfa, Medenine). The method won El Alamein in 1942 and ground down German armour around Caen in 1944, which made the American breakout possible. Sea control kept Britain fed and enabled Sicily, Italy and Normandy.
whereItFailed: France and Dunkirk 1940; Greece and Crete 1941; Singapore, February 1942, where about 80,000 Commonwealth troops surrendered to a smaller Japanese force; repeated desert armour defeats (Battleaxe 1941, Gazala and the fall of Tobruk June 1942) from poor tank-infantry-artillery cooperation and inferior antitank guns; slow, costly fighting around Caen (Goodwood, July 1944); Arnhem, September 1944, when Market Garden outran its logistics and ran into SS panzer units.

sources.title: House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 4 'The British Response, 1940-42' and 'War in the Desert'
Hart, Montgomery and 'Colossal Cracks': The 21st Army Group in Northwest Europe, 1944-45 (Praeger, 2000)
French, Raising Churchill's Army: The British Army and the War against Germany 1919-1945 (OUP, 2000)

name: Byzantine army of the Strategikon and the military manuals (c. 600-1071)

weightNotes.aggression: The manuals counsel against risking a pitched battle unless the odds are clearly favourable and prefer to hurt the enemy by deceit, raids and hunger (Strategikon books VII-VIII, Dennis tr.); Byzantine tactics 'mostly relied on skirmishing and ambushes' as 'a deliberate and consistent strategy' to preserve scarce men (Byzantine army page). Offensives existed (10th-century reconquest, Basil II), so not lower.
weightNotes.maneuver: A cavalry army built around mobility, ambush (Strategikon book IV) and shadowing of raiders (De velitatione, c. 970: 'skirmishing and guerrilla-type border warfare'). Kleidion (1014) was won by sending Xiphias round the mountain into the Bulgarian rear.
weightNotes.flanking: The standard cavalry array had flank guards and outflanking detachments (Strategikon book II-III); Belisarius at Dara (530) placed Heruli in ambush off his flank; Kleidion was a rear attack (Dara, Kleidion pages).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Book X is devoted to sieges and the 10th-century offensives took fortresses methodically, but the defensive system rested on holding fortified places and letting raiders exhaust themselves (Haldon 1999). Balanced.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The manual's battle order puts a second line behind the first so a beaten first line can fall back and reform, plus a rear guard and baggage guard (Strategikon II; Haldon). Manzikert (1071) shows the cost when the reserve commander, Andronikos Doukas, marched away instead (Manzikert page).
weightNotes.scouting: Scouts, spies and surprise attacks are whole books of the Strategikon (IX) and De velitatione builds the border defence on watch posts and early warning (De velitatione page). High.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Low by evidence, not inverted: Manzikert 1071, the army broke with 'relatively low' losses and 'many units survived the battle intact' once Doukas's reserve marched off without casualties (Manzikert page); Achelous 917, the 60,000-strong army dissolved when its battle order loosened in pursuit and a rumour spread that Leo Phokas was dead (Achelous page). The Strategikon's two-line order expected the first line to fall back on the second early. No battle gives a numeric loss share at the break; 0.09 is a judgment for an early, mostly intact disengagement.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Lancer-archer cavalry with Avar-pattern kit, heavy and light infantry with bows and slings, specialised menavlatoi against enemy kataphraktoi, siege engineers (Byzantine army page). Cavalry-centred, so not higher.
weightNotes.initiative: Command was by manual and by the general; tagma and meros commanders had set drills. Thematic commanders acted on their own against raids, but battle plans were centralised. Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Strategikon book V regulates baggage trains, a fortified intermediate camp and about four days' supply; nightly fortified camps (Strategikon page; Haldon 1999, logistics chapters). Operations stayed within supply.

summary: A professional, largely cavalry army whose method was written down: the Strategikon (c. 600), Leo VI's Taktika and the 10th-century manuals. Lancer-archer cavalry deployed in two lines with flank guards and outflankers; infantry held fortified camps and defiles. Strategy was economical: avoid an even pitched battle, shadow raiders, ambush them on the way home, rely on fortified towns and the thematic system, and fight only on favourable terms or after the enemy was worn down by hunger and harassment.
whyItWorked: Doctrine matched the empire's chronic shortage of men: preserving the army mattered more than winning any one battle, and the manuals codified ambush, feigned flight and two-line cavalry tactics drawn from Avar, Persian and Arab enemies. Dara (530) and Kleidion (1014, Samuel's army trapped by an attack from the rear and thousands blinded afterwards) show the method under good commanders; the 10th-century eastern reconquest showed it could also attack.
whereItFailed: When politics split the command: at Manzikert (1071) Doukas ignored the order to cover the withdrawal, the rear guard of levies fled, and the professional core was destroyed. At Achelous (917) Simeon's Bulgarians routed the army completely. Dependence on mercenaries and court politics after 1025 eroded the thematic base that the doctrine assumed.

sources.title: Dennis (tr.), Maurice's Strategikon: Handbook of Byzantine Military Strategy (1984)
Dennis, Three Byzantine Military Treatises (Dumbarton Oaks, 1985)
Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World 565-1204 (UCL Press, 1999)

name: Carthaginian army under Hannibal (218-202 BC)

weightNotes.aggression: Invaded Italy over the Alps in 218 and sought battle three times in three years (Trebia, Trasimene, Cannae; Second Punic War pages). Not higher because after Cannae he never marched on Rome and from 207 sat 'undefeated but ineffective' in Bruttium (Zama page).
weightNotes.maneuver: Operational manoeuvre was the method: the Alpine crossing, the march round Fabius, and the Trasimene ambush, 'widely considered a unique occurrence' of a whole army destroyed by ambush (Trasimene page; Lazenby, Hannibal's War).
weightNotes.flanking: Every great victory was an envelopment: Mago's 2,000 hidden in a watercourse hit the Roman rear at the Trebia; at Cannae the Africans on the wings closed on the Roman flanks while the cavalry took the rear (Cannae, Trebia pages). Near maximum.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Saguntum (219) took eight months; in Italy he had no siege train and never besieged Rome; Hasdrubal was bringing 'siege equipment' when destroyed at the Metaurus (Metaurus page). Field battle was the strategy.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Held forces out of sight or out of the fight until the decisive moment: Mago's ambush party at the Trebia, the uncommitted African infantry at Cannae, the veteran third line kept 200 m back at Zama (Zama page). Moderate fraction.
weightNotes.scouting: Hannibal read Roman commanders and ground well (Flaminius lured into the Trasimene defile; Numidian screens). Lowered because neither Hannibal nor Hasdrubal detected Nero's forced march before the Metaurus (Metaurus page).
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Hannibal's own army held to destruction rather than withdraw: Zama 202 BC, about 100% (Polybius: 20,000 killed and as many captured, 'the entire Carthaginian army', Zama page); Metaurus 207 BC, Hasdrubal's army routed after being outflanked with 15,400 killed or captured and Hasdrubal dead (army size only from ancient figures, so no reliable share; Metaurus page). In victory it absorbed losses without breaking: Cannae 216 BC, about 11% (Polybius 5,700 dead of roughly 50,000, Cannae page) while the centre gave ground on orders. Allied first-line and new levies at Zama broke earlier (no figure). 0.6: holds until largely destroyed.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Libyan heavy foot, Iberian and Gallic line infantry, Balearic slingers, Iberian and Gallic heavy horse, Numidian javelin horse and elephants, each with a defined role (Military of Carthage, Cannae pages).
weightNotes.initiative: Subordinates (Mago, Maharbal, Hasdrubal of the cavalry) executed timed independent parts of the plan, but the system depended on Hannibal personally; other Carthaginian generals in Spain and Africa were repeatedly beaten (Zama page). Middling.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Lived off Italy for 15 years with almost no seaborne resupply; lost heavily crossing the Alps (13,000 men in the two-month campaign, Alps page); Fabius's strategy targeted his foraging (Fabian strategy page). Operations ignored supply limits.

summary: A multinational professional army (African, Iberian, Gallic and Numidian contingents, with elephants) commanded personally by Hannibal. It invaded Italy overland, lived off the country, and sought battle on ground Hannibal chose: Numidian horse lured the Romans across the Trebia, the whole army ambushed a consular army on the march at Lake Trasimene, and at Cannae a deliberately yielding infantry centre drew the Roman mass forward while African infantry closed the flanks and the cavalry sealed the rear. It lacked a siege train and the political base to convert victories into the surrender of Rome.
whyItWorked: Superior cavalry and a commander who used terrain, deception and timing better than any opponent until Scipio; the yielding centre at Cannae (216 BC, at least 67,500 Romans killed or captured per the Zama page summary) is the classic double envelopment. Mixed contingents were given tasks that matched their arms, and the army stayed loyal through 15 years far from home.
whereItFailed: Could not take fortified cities or force Rome to negotiate; the Fabian strategy of shadowing and denying forage wore it down. When Hasdrubal's relief army was caught and destroyed at the Metaurus (207 BC, 15,400 killed or captured), Hannibal was confined to Bruttium. At Zama (202 BC) Scipio had the better cavalry (Masinissa's Numidians); the Carthaginian horse was driven off, returned Roman cavalry hit the veteran line in the rear and the army was destroyed.

sources.title: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps, Wikipedia
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (University of Oklahoma Press, 1998)

name: French methodical battle and the Maginot Line (1939-1940)

weightNotes.aggression: Defensive mindset reinforced by the Maginot Line (House ch. 3); the September 1939 Saar offensive advanced a few kilometres and withdrew. Attack only after careful, methodical preparation to minimise casualties (1921 Provisional Instructions, quoted in House ch. 3).
weightNotes.maneuver: Bataille conduite: a tightly controlled set-piece battle where all units advance methodically according to an elaborate plan (House ch. 3; Doughty, Seeds of Disaster). Attrition and firepower, not movement.
weightNotes.flanking: The 1936 regulation's 'defensive without thought of retreat' meant rigid orientation to the front rather than manoeuvring against flank or rear (House ch. 3). The Dyle-Breda advance into Belgium was a forward move into prepared lines, not a flanking manoeuvre.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Doctrine was terrain-oriented: hold and fortify lines (Maginot Line, Dyle line) rather than seek the enemy field army. Middle value because the engine weighs cities against formations, and French objectives were ground, not armies.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Doctrine wanted a large general reserve, but in practice the Breda variant sent Seventh Army, the main reserve, to Holland, the four armoured divisions were scattered behind the front and broken up when committed (House ch. 4). Practice, not paper, sets the weight.
weightNotes.scouting: Air reconnaissance saw the German columns in the Ardennes on 10-12 May but the High Command discounted it; radio use was restricted for fear of signals intelligence (House ch. 3). Low-moderate.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: 'Defensive without thought of retreat' (1936 regulation, House ch. 3): units were told to hold in place, so the good-order withdrawal point is set high; actual collapses (55th Division at Sedan) belong to cohesion in the snapshot, not doctrine.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Doctrine assigned artillery, tanks and aviation to support the infantry, but 36 tank battalions were dispersed among infantry armies without joint training and air support was mostly reconnaissance (House ch. 3-4). Paper combined arms, poor practice.
weightNotes.initiative: Doughty locates the main cause of 1940 in overcentralisation; command moved at First World War pace and radios were to be used only when no other means existed (House ch. 3).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Methodical battle meant no attack before artillery, ammunition and supply were in place; operations never outran supply. Very high.

summary: The French Army of 1939-40 kept the lessons of 1918: firepower kills, so attack only in carefully prepared, centrally controlled set-piece battles where the infantry advances by bounds under massed artillery, with tanks parcelled out in support. The frontier was covered by the Maginot Line, which freed men for a planned advance into Belgium to fight on the Dyle with the British. Command was centralised and slow, radios were distrusted, armoured divisions were few and formed late, and the army was a mobilised militia needing months to train (House ch. 3).
whyItWorked: It won 1918 and it worked where the enemy attacked prepared positions on French terms: the Maginot Line was never broken frontally in May-June 1940, and the Cavalry Corps at Hannut and First Army at Gembloux (12-15 May) stopped German panzer corps in set-piece defence. Its firepower and casualty-saving logic suited a country with a smaller population than Germany.
whereItFailed: Sedan, 13-15 May 1940: the main German mechanised mass came through the Ardennes against two weak reserve divisions at the hinge of the Allied line. The French could not plan and launch counterattacks fast enough (XXI Corps' counterattack of 14 May dissolved into static stop-lines), the general reserve had been sent to Holland, and once panzers were loose in the rear the centrally controlled system could not redeploy in time. France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940, six weeks after the offensive began.

sources.title: House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), ch. 3-4 (French doctrine, 1940 campaign)
Doughty, The Seeds of Disaster: The Development of French Army Doctrine, 1919-1939 (Archon, 1985), catalogue record
Review of Doughty, The Seeds of Disaster (History of War)
Roncolato, 'Methodical Battle Didn't Work Then', US Naval Institute Proceedings 122/2 (1996)

name: German Bewegungskrieg and Auftragstaktik (1939-1941)

weightNotes.aggression: Offensive, short-war doctrine: Poland, Norway, France, Balkans and USSR were all opened by German attacks; the 1945 War Department handbook calls German leadership 'aggressive and daring' (TM-E 30-451 ch. IV).
weightNotes.maneuver: Kesselschlacht: panzer groups penetrated and closed pincers behind enemy armies (Minsk, Kiev, Vyazma 1941); House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare ch. 4 'The German Advance in Russia'.
weightNotes.flanking: Sichelschnitt 1940 put 7 of 10 panzer divisions through the Ardennes on a 70 km front against the weak hinge of the Allied line (House ch. 4; Frieser, Blitzkrieg Legend).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Targets were enemy field armies; cities were bypassed and left to the infantry (Warsaw, where 57 tanks were lost in one day, taught that tanks should avoid urban fighting; House ch. 4). Leningrad 1941 was invested rather than stormed.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Germany fought 1939-41 with almost everything forward and no real strategic reserve; panzer corps lacked the infantry to seal their own encirclements (House ch. 4). Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Armoured reconnaissance battalions and Luftwaffe air reconnaissance were good tactically (TM-E 30-451 ch. IV), but strategic intelligence badly underrated Soviet reserves and mobilisation capacity in 1941.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: High unit cohesion and battlegroup (Kampfgruppe) improvisation kept depleted formations fighting; judgment, kept below typical WWII breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Panzer divisions habitually task-organised tanks, motorised infantry, artillery, engineers and flak into battlegroups (House ch. 4); Luftwaffe close support at Sedan 1940. Not 1.0 because air-ground coordination was poor in Poland and most infantry divisions stayed horse-drawn.
weightNotes.initiative: Auftragstaktik: orders gave the intent and left the method to subordinates; 'German tactical doctrines stress the responsibility and the initiative of subordinates' (TM-E 30-451 ch. IV). Commanders led from the front (Guderian, Rommel).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The army was geared to short distances, tied to railheads and horse transport with repairs sent back to Germany; panzer spearheads outran supply and maintenance in Russia 1941 (House ch. 4). Operations routinely exceeded supply.

summary: Germany concentrated its few panzer and motorised divisions into large masses at a decisive point, broke through with infantry, engineers, artillery and dive bombers, then drove the mobile divisions deep into the enemy rear to cut communications and encircle whole armies while the foot infantry followed to reduce the pockets. The Luftwaffe first won air superiority, then interdicted and supported the spearheads. Command was decentralised: commanders received an intent and acted on their own judgment, led from the front, and used radio in every tank to react faster than opponents could. 'Blitzkrieg' was not a formal doctrine; it was traditional Prussian Bewegungskrieg (war of movement) given engines and radios.
whyItWorked: Opponents deployed in linear cordons without depth or mobile reserves and commanded at First World War speed, so deep penetrations paralysed them psychologically and organisationally (House ch. 4). Poland fell in about five weeks, France and the Low Countries in six, and the 1941 encirclements destroyed most of the pre-war Red Army. Concentration, not superior tank numbers, was decisive: the Allies had more and often better tanks in 1940.
whereItFailed: The system assumed short campaigns. In Russia 1941 distances, mud and worn-out vehicles broke the logistics; encirclements leaked because panzer corps could not seal them; Soviet reserves were far larger than estimated, and the offensive stalled before Moscow in December 1941 and was thrown back by the Soviet counteroffensive. Against an enemy with depth and antitank strength the method stopped working (Kursk 1943). It could not cross the Channel (Battle of Britain 1940), and in North Africa supply across the Mediterranean, not tactics, set the limit.

name: Classical Greek hoplite warfare

weightNotes.aggression: Hanson (Western Way of War): invaders ravaged farmland to force a short, decisive pitched battle, which defenders usually accepted. Above mid, not higher because many campaigns ended in ravaging without battle.
weightNotes.maneuver: Two phalanxes met head-on on level ground; the decision came by collision and shoving (othismos). Near-pure attrition.
weightNotes.flanking: Flanking was mostly incidental: the rightward drift of lines (Mantinea 418) let the strong right wing overlap. Deliberate schemes (Leuctra 371, Theban column at least fifty shields deep) were late exceptions.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Poor at assault; cities fell by blockade or betrayal over months or years (Potidaea, Plataea 429-427). Armies preferred ravaging to provoke battle.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The whole phalanx was committed at once; held-back reserves are nearly absent before the 4th century.
weightNotes.scouting: Little cavalry in most poleis; Sparta's mora was caught in the open by peltasts at Lechaeum (390). Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Krentz (GRBS 1985): defeated hoplite armies typically lost 10-20% killed (average about 14%, including the pursuit), victors about 5%. The break therefore came at well under 10% loss; 0.08.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Hoplites decided battles; psiloi, archers and cavalry were marginal until peltasts and cavalry grew in the 4th century (Lechaeum, Sphacteria).
weightNotes.initiative: Sparta's layered officer chain gave tactical responsiveness; most poleis were citizen militias with elected generals and little drill. Weighted average 0.3.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Short-range, short-season campaigns: citizens brought a few days' rations and relied on markets and plunder, so operations stayed near home and ended when food or the season ran out.

summary: Citizen heavy infantry (hoplites with large round shield, spear and bronze armour) fought in a close-order phalanx usually eight deep. Campaigns were short summer invasions of a neighbour's farmland intended to provoke a single pitched battle on level ground, decided within hours by collision and push; the victor held the field and set up a trophy, and pursuit was limited. Light troops, cavalry and sieges were secondary; Sparta was the professional exception within the same system.
whyItWorked: The phalanx was very hard to break frontally on open ground, and heavily armoured hoplites outclassed lightly protected missile infantry at close quarters, as at Marathon and Plataea. The system matched the economics of farmer-citizen states: short, decisive and cheap.
whereItFailed: On broken ground or against light troops who refused contact: Sphacteria (425), where Spartans were worn down by archers and psiloi and the survivors surrendered; Lechaeum (390), where Iphicrates's peltasts killed about 250 of a 600-man Spartan mora with minimal losses. Against a concentrated, deep attack on one point: Leuctra (371). In long wars, its inability to take cities or campaign out of season made the Peloponnesian War a war of blockades and fleets.

sources.title: Krentz, Casualties in Hoplite Battles, GRBS 26 (1985)
Hanson, The Western Way of War (2nd ed. 2000)

name: Han dynasty imperial army (c. 200 BC - AD 100)

weightNotes.aggression: Under Emperor Wu the Han took the war to the steppe: Longcheng raid 129 BC, Hexi and Ordos campaigns, Mobei 119 BC, Dayuan 104-102 BC, Zhizhi 36 BC, Dou Xian's 50,000 cavalry in AD 89 (Han-Xiongnu War pages). Lowered because the first seventy years after Baideng (200 BC) were heqin appeasement.
weightNotes.maneuver: Long-distance cavalry expeditions in multiple columns (Mobei: two columns of 50,000 cavalry), but the infantry core fought positionally from wagon laagers (Mobei page). Middling-high.
weightNotes.flanking: At Mobei the Han shock cavalry 'encircled the Chanyu's army from both flanks' under cover of a sandstorm, and Lu Bode's division took a flanking route; Li Guang's flanking column got lost and missed the battle (Mobei page).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Capable of sieges (Dayuan 102 BC: engineers diverted the river and cut the city's water; Zhizhi 36 BC: citadel stormed and burned), but the strategic target was the nomad field army (War of the Heavenly Horses, Zhizhi pages).
weightNotes.reserveUse: Wei Qing held 5,000 cavalry inside the wagon ring to deal with breakthroughs before committing it to the envelopment (Mobei page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Frontier beacon and watch-post system with careful records (Military of the Han page), but in the field intelligence failed often: a prisoner's misinformation reshuffled the Mobei columns, Li Guang got lost, Gaozu was lured into encirclement at Baideng (200 BC).
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. The one quantified case held to near destruction: Li Ling 99 BC, 5,000 infantry encircled by 30,000-80,000 Xiongnu fought a days-long retreat, ran out of arrows and surrendered with only 400 escaping, about 92% lost (Li Ling page). Han law executed generals who failed (Military of the Han page), which pushed commanders to hold. Single episode of a detached force, and conscript or penal armies (first Dayuan expedition) dissolved through starvation rather than battle, so 0.5 rather than higher.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Crossbow infantry, armoured war wagons (wugang chariots), cavalry and archers in one formation; at Mobei the wagon ring sheltered archers, crossbowmen and infantry while cavalry manoeuvred (Mobei page). The crossbow gave Han forces a 'slight advantage' (Military of the Han page).
weightNotes.initiative: Column commanders operated weeks apart in the steppe, but under heavy penalties for failure and with the emperor redirecting columns (Mobei); Li Guang's suicide shows the system punished, not rewarded, independent judgment.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Expeditions needed huge trains (second Dayuan expedition: 60,000 men with 100,000 oxen and 20,000 donkeys and camels; it still returned with only 10,000 men), the first Dayuan army starved, and frontier military colonies grew grain for garrisons (War of the Heavenly Horses, Military of the Han pages). Planned but often exceeded.

summary: A large state army, initially conscript and later mostly professional, with a standing force of 600,000-700,000 including about 300,000 cavalry by the late 2nd century BC (Military of the Han page). The infantry fought in deep formations with crossbows and halberds, often behind laagers of armoured war wagons; the cavalry, built up to fight the Xiongnu, made long expeditions into the steppe in converging columns. The frontier was held by walls, beacons and military colonies, and campaigns were organised by a literate bureaucracy that tracked rations and equipment.
whyItWorked: Organisation and resources: the Han could raise, equip and supply forces far larger than any nomad confederation and combine crossbow firepower from a wagon fortress with massed cavalry. Mobei (119 BC) broke the Chanyu's main army, the Hexi corridor and Western Regions were secured, and Zhizhi (36 BC) killed a Xiongnu chanyu far beyond the frontier.
whereItFailed: Distance and supply: the first Dayuan expedition (104 BC) starved, and even the successful second one came back with 10,000 of 60,000 men. Infantry caught in the steppe without support was destroyed (Li Ling, 99 BC). Intelligence failures and the emperor's interference split commands (Baideng 200 BC, the Mobei column switch), and horse losses on each expedition were ruinous.

Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (Harvard UP, 2007)

name: Israel Defense Forces in the Six-Day War (1967)

weightNotes.aggression: Pre-emptive war: Operation Focus struck the Arab air forces on the morning of 5 June, followed at once by the ground offensive; Tal's armour corps was trained for 'high mobility and relentless assault' (Operation Focus, Israel Tal pages; Oren, Six Days of War).
weightNotes.maneuver: Armoured divisions broke through and drove deep: Rafah was circumvented, the Sinai was taken and the Suez Canal reached within the six days (Six-Day War page; van Creveld, Sword and the Olive).
weightNotes.flanking: At Abu-Ageila Sharon's division landed paratroopers by helicopter to silence the Egyptian artillery in the rear while armour and infantry attacked at night (Abu-Ageila page); Rafah was bypassed. High.
weightNotes.siegePreference: No sieges: fortified localities were stormed or bypassed in a war of days. Near zero.
weightNotes.reserveUse: A mobilised reserve army committed almost entirely to three fronts in sequence, with the air force switched between them; little held back (Six-Day War page; Pollack). Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Intelligence on Arab air bases made Operation Focus possible, destroying about 450 aircraft by noon on the first day (Operation Focus page). 1973's intelligence failure is a different era of this force, so 1967 rates high.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. No IDF unit withdrawal is recorded in 1967, so there is no share at withdrawal: attacks were pressed through losses, e.g. the 7th Armoured Brigade cleared Khan Yunis 'despite heavy losses' (Six-Day War page, Oren) and paratroopers took Ammunition Hill, a 150-man Jordanian position, trench by trench with 36 killed (Ammunition Hill page). Israel's total dead for the war were 776-983. 0.25 is a judgment above observed losses for a force that rarely needed to withdraw.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Abu-Ageila was a model night combined-arms attack (infantry, paratroopers, tanks, artillery), and air supremacy enabled air-ground support. But Tal's doctrine emphasised the tank, and that imbalance failed in 1973 when piecemeal armoured counterattacks were beaten by infantry anti-tank missiles (Abu-Ageila, Yom Kippur War pages). 0.6.
weightNotes.initiative: Commanders led from the front and exploited opportunities without waiting for orders; van Creveld (Command in War) uses the Israeli army as his modern example of decentralised command. Gonen entrusted the Rafah breakthrough to a single battalion (Six-Day War page).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: A short-war army: divisions drove to the canal on what they carried, with logistics improvised behind them (van Creveld, Sword and the Olive). Operations were not limited by supply planning in 1967. Low-middling.

summary: A small standing cadre and a large, quickly mobilised reserve army, fighting on interior lines against several neighbours. Doctrine stressed the pre-emptive offensive, winning air superiority first and then concentrating armoured divisions for deep breakthroughs, with commanders leading from the front and acting on intent. In 1967 the air force destroyed most of the Egyptian air force on the ground by noon of the first day, then the army took Sinai, the West Bank and the Golan Heights in six days.
whyItWorked: Surprise and air superiority on the first morning (about 452 aircraft destroyed in Operation Focus), excellent long-range tank gunnery (Tal retrained gunners to hit beyond 1.5 km), and aggressive decentralised command against Arab armies whose junior officers showed little initiative (Pollack, Arabs at War). Abu-Ageila showed a well-coordinated night attack against prepared defences.
whereItFailed: Its 1967 success hardened into overconfidence in the tank and in intelligence: in October 1973 the surprise attack succeeded, and armoured counterattacks from 6 to 8 October were 'piecemeal and inadequately supported' and beaten by Egyptian infantry with RPGs and Sagger missiles (Yom Kippur War page). The doctrine depends on a short war, air supremacy and early warning; without them its small army was costly to sustain.
