name: Regio Esercito doctrine (1940-1943)

weightNotes.aggression: Mussolini ordered offensives (Alps June 1940, Egypt September 1940, Greece October 1940), but field commanders were cautious: Graziani halted at Sidi Barrani after about 100 km and dug in for three months (Christie, DTIC ADA367611). Below middle.
weightNotes.maneuver: The 1938 'guerra di rapido corso' doctrine envisaged mechanised manoeuvre (Christie), but most formations were heavy infantry divisions 'similar to those employed in World War I', on foot, so practice was slow and positional.
weightNotes.flanking: Little outflanking in practice; Graziani did not use the motorised manoeuvre he had pioneered in Ethiopia (Christie). Low.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Fortified camps and static positions (Sidi Barrani camps 1940; Tobruk siege 1941 alongside the Germans); terrain-holding rather than seeking the enemy army.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Formations were spread across fortified camps with weak mobile reserves (House ch. 4 on Compass). Low-moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: O'Connor's Compass attack of December 1940 achieved surprise against the camps; air reconnaissance and radio intelligence were weak. Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Many formations withdrew or surrendered early once outflanked (Beda Fomm, February 1941); others fought hard (Ariete at Bir el Gobi 1941, Folgore at El Alamein 1942). Low value; most of the variation belongs in snapshot cohesion.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Binary two-regiment divisions, L3 tankettes, few radios and little armour-infantry-artillery training; the industrial base could not equip mechanised formations (House ch. 3; Christie).
weightNotes.initiative: Rigid, centralised command and a gulf between officers and men (Knox, Hitler's Italian Allies). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Graziani refused to advance until roads, water and supplies were in place; but Greece was invaded in 1940 with little preparation, and North Africa was always limited by Mediterranean convoys. Middle.

summary: Italy entered the war with an army designed for a short war of manoeuvre on paper (the 1938 'guerra di rapido corso', derived from the motorised columns of the Ethiopian war) but equipped and trained as a First World War infantry army: binary divisions on foot, light tanks and tankettes, few radios, little fuel and a weak industrial base. In practice Italian forces advanced cautiously, then fortified camps and lines and waited for supply. From 1941 most Italian divisions in North Africa fought under German operational direction, where several did well.
whyItWorked: Against weak or poorly armed opponents (Ethiopia 1935-36) motorised columns and air power worked. Under German direction in 1941-42, Italian armoured and parachute divisions fought effectively (Ariete at Bir el Gobi, November 1941; Folgore at El Alamein, October 1942), and the navy's frogmen crippled two British battleships at Alexandria in December 1941.
whereItFailed: Alps, June 1940: small gains against weak French forces at heavy cost. Greece, October 1940: invasion launched without preparation, thrown back into Albania. Compass, December 1940 to February 1941: the British destroyed the 10th Army in its fortified camps and cut off its retreat at Beda Fomm, taking about 130,000 prisoners. East Africa 1941. Taranto and Cape Matapan at sea. The Italian Eighth Army on the Don collapsed in Operation Little Saturn, December 1942; Sicily, July 1943.

Knox, Hitler's Italian Allies: Royal Armed Forces, Fascist Regime, and the War of 1940-1943 (Cambridge UP, 2000)

name: Imperial Japanese Army and Navy doctrine (1941-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: 'The Japanese seem to feel that there is some mystic virtue in the attack'; officers chose to attack even where orthodox tactics demanded defence (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII). Every infantry manual 1909-1945 stressed the offensive (Drea, Nomonhan, ch. 1).
weightNotes.maneuver: Sokusen sokketsu: short, decisive war by encirclement using mobility, night movement and concentration (Drea, Nomonhan). Malaya 1941-42 was fast infiltration down the peninsula; island battles later were static. Moderately high.
weightNotes.flanking: 'The envelopment is the preferred form of attack'; the Japanese tried double envelopments even without numerical superiority, and sent small forces round to the enemy rear (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Took fortresses and bases when they were the objective (Hong Kong, Singapore, Bataan and Corregidor), but doctrine aimed at the enemy force. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Advance guards took a third to a half of a division's infantry and units were committed in full (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII); piecemeal commitment on Guadalcanal. Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Good pre-war intelligence for Malaya, but chronic underestimation of the enemy: Ichiki's detachment of about 900 attacked a Marine division on Guadalcanal, and late carrier scouting contributed to Midway. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke: garrisons fought to annihilation. Iwo Jima 1945: of 21,000 defenders only 216 were taken prisoner, about 99% lost (Iwo Jima page); Attu 1943: over 2,351 lost and 28 prisoners, the last in a banzai charge, about 99% (Attu page); Tarawa 1943: the 4,500 defenders fought almost to the last man (Tarawa page). Surrender and retreat were dishonourable; the 1932 manual told commanders forced to withdraw to regain the offensive (Drea). Corrected 2026-10-30: 0.1 -> 0.95.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Training stressed 'infantry tactics as opposed to combined arms tactics' and spiritual training to compensate for weak artillery and armour (Drea, Nomonhan). Naval aviation was strong, which keeps it above the floor.
weightNotes.initiative: Commanders and staffs operated well forward and junior officers were aggressive (TM-E 30-480 ch. VII); offset by rigid adherence to complex plans (Midway) and insubordination at the top (Kwantung Army).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Operations routinely outran supply: Guadalcanal ('Starvation Island'), Imphal 1944 where troops were expected to live on captured stores, New Guinea. Very low.

summary: An infantry army and a carrier navy built for a short, decisive war. The army relied on surprise, envelopment, night attack and the spirit of the offensive to compensate for weak artillery, armour and industry; commanders attacked even against superior forces and treated defence as a temporary state. The navy built a powerful carrier striking force and trained intensively for night surface combat with long-range torpedoes. Logistics was an afterthought. From 1944 the army switched to fortified defence in depth on islands (caves and bunkers on Peleliu, Iwo Jima, Okinawa) designed to bleed the attacker, still ending in suicidal counterattacks.
whyItWorked: Against unprepared colonial garrisons in 1941-42 speed, surprise and infiltration were overwhelming: Pearl Harbor, the Philippines, Malaya and Singapore (February 1942) fell within months. Night actions such as Savo Island (August 1942) showed the navy's training edge. The 1944-45 island defences inflicted very heavy US casualties (Iwo Jima, Okinawa).
whereItFailed: Nomonhan 1939, where Soviet combined arms crushed infantry spirit; Midway, June 1942, four fleet carriers lost through poor scouting and an over-complex plan; Guadalcanal, August 1942 to February 1943, where piecemeal night attacks (Tenaru, Bloody Ridge) broke on prepared Marine positions and starvation and disease killed more men than combat; Imphal-Kohima 1944, an offensive launched without supply that cost most of the Fifteenth Army; banzai charges at Attu and Saipan; Leyte Gulf, October 1944.

name: Macedonian combined arms (Philip II and Alexander)

weightNotes.aggression: Alexander attacked at once at the Granicus, sought out Darius at Issus and Gaugamela and pursued him across Iran; offensive at every level.
weightNotes.maneuver: Oblique advance to the right at Gaugamela to pull Persian cavalry out of line; the night crossing of the monsoon-swollen Hydaspes to take Porus in the flank. Manoeuvre-leaning but still fought set-piece battles.
weightNotes.flanking: The Companion cavalry, in wedge formation, was the hammer that struck into a gap or flank while the phalanx held (Companion cavalry article; Gaugamela).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Took every Persian naval base before marching inland (Tyre 332 by mole and ship-borne engines, Gaza), yet the aim was always the decisive field battle with the king. Balanced.
weightNotes.reserveUse: At Gaugamela a second line was posted to face about against envelopment; otherwise most of the army was committed. Moderate-low.
weightNotes.scouting: Prodromoi light cavalry screened and scouted; Engels shows campaigns planned on intelligence about harvests, water and routes. Above mid.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Professional, long-serving phalangites and Companions with high cohesion; under Alexander they did not break in a pitched battle. 0.1, below the ancient breakpoint range.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Sarissa phalanx, hypaspists, Companion and Thessalian heavy cavalry, light cavalry, Agrianian javelinmen, Cretan archers and a siege train used together in one plan. The ancient benchmark.
weightNotes.initiative: Parmenion commanded the left independently and detachments (Craterus at the Hydaspes) acted on their own; but the decisive blow depended on Alexander leading it in person.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Engels (Alexander and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army): Philip cut the baggage train and carts, soldiers carried their own kit, routes were timed to harvests and fleet supply. The Gedrosian march (325) is the exception that proves the cost.

summary: Philip II built a professional army around a deep phalanx of pikemen with the 5-6 m sarissa, which fixed the enemy line frontally (the anvil), while heavy shock cavalry led by the king (the Companions) struck the decisive blow into a flank or a gap (the hammer). Light infantry, archers and Thessalian cavalry covered the joints and the other wing. A lean baggage train and a siege corps let it march fast and take fortified cities. Alexander added operational daring: rapid pursuits, river crossings and sieges of island cities.
whyItWorked: Each arm covered the others' weakness: the phalanx pinned the enemy and held the defensive wing, the cavalry exploited the moment, light troops protected the flanks. Professional drill and Engels-style logistics gave speed and staying power; siege capability meant no fortress could stop a campaign.
whereItFailed: The system depended on the cavalry and the king: without them the phalanx alone was brittle on rough ground and against flexible infantry. Cynoscephalae (197) and Pydna (168): Roman maniples exploited gaps when the phalanx lost cohesion on uneven ground and attacked its exposed flanks. Under Alexander, logistics overreach in the Gedrosian desert (325) cost heavy losses outside battle.

sources.title: Engels, Alexander the Great and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army (1978)

name: Mongol Empire steppe warfare

weightNotes.aggression: Strategically relentless offensives (Khwarazm 1219-21, Rus 1237-40, Hungary and Poland 1241, Baghdad 1258), but tactically they declined fights on bad terms, so not 1.0.
weightNotes.maneuver: Pure manoeuvre: every man mounted with three or four horses, multiple columns, deep raids and envelopment (May, Mongol Art of War).
weightNotes.flanking: Encirclement was the standard battle plan; at Legnica (1241) feigned attacks and withdrawals by dispersed groups drew the enemy away from its main body into ambush.
weightNotes.siegePreference: They destroyed the field army first, then took cities systematically with captured and hired engineers (Xiangyang 1273, counterweight trebuchets built by Persian and Syrian engineers). Field battle first, siege second.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Commanders held back heavy cavalry to receive an enemy drawn on by the feigned retreat (Kalka 1223, Mohi 1241); moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Screens of scouts far ahead and pre-war intelligence: Subutai sent spies into Poland, Hungary and eastern Austria before 1241. Best in era.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Mongol units broke contact early rather than accept attritional losses, then returned; the feigned retreat is the extreme form. Low threshold = early disengagement, not fragility.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Light horse archers, heavy lancers, conscripted infantry and Chinese and Persian siege engineers with gunpowder weapons (Khwarazm campaign order of battle). Infantry weak, so not higher.
weightNotes.initiative: Decimal units (tumen of 10,000) under commanders who operated independently for years across continents (Jebe and Subutai 1220-23), coordinated by the yam relay. High.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies moved with their herds and remounts and lived off pasture and plunder, so they ranged far beyond any supply network (low strictness), yet campaigns were timed to grass and halted when pasture failed. 0.45.

summary: A fully mounted army organised in decimal units (10, 100, 1,000, 10,000) with three or four horses per man. Columns advanced on a broad front, separated by days but converging on a target, after long intelligence preparation. In battle, light horse archers wore down and disordered the enemy with arrows and feigned withdrawals, drawing pursuers into envelopment and a final charge by heavy lancers. Fortified cities were taken by conscripted labour and Chinese and Persian engineers with trebuchets and gunpowder weapons, and resistance was punished by massacre to induce surrender elsewhere.
whyItWorked: Mobility and remounts gave them the choice of where and when to fight; superior scouting and intelligence meant they usually knew more than the enemy; discipline and decimal organisation let dispersed columns coordinate over hundreds of kilometres; adopting foreign siege engineering removed the classic nomad weakness against walls.
whereItFailed: Against an enemy who used their own methods with better local knowledge and numbers: Ain Jalut (1260), where Baibars's feigned retreat drew Kitbuqa's reduced force into an ambush in the hills. Where horses and pasture could not follow: the invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) were wrecked at sea by typhoons and stopped on the beaches; Syria and Vietnam campaigns were limited by grazing and climate. Succession politics also halted campaigns (withdrawal from Hungary 1242).

Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire, Wikipedia
Battle of the Kalka River, Wikipedia
May, The Mongol Art of War (2007)

name: Mughal imperial army (1526-1739)

weightNotes.aggression: Expansion was continuous from Babur to Aurangzeb (Panipat 1526, Chittor 1567-68, the Deccan campaigns 1681-1707), but Gommans (Mughal Warfare) stresses that much of it was won by negotiation, co-option and siege rather than battle. Moderately high.
weightNotes.maneuver: The army moved as a vast camp-city: at Karnal (1739) a war camp of about 300,000 including non-combatants, 3,000 guns and 2,000 elephants, which spent a month encamped outside Delhi before moving (Karnal page). Slow; Babur's small 1526 army was the exception.
weightNotes.flanking: Turko-Mongol tulughma flank attacks: at Panipat (1526) 'musket and cannon pinned Ibrahim's centre while horse archers harried the flanks and rear' (Panipat page).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Siege was the main form of war (Gommans): Chittor took four months with 5,000 builders digging sabats and mines (Chittorgarh page); in the Deccan, Ramsej alone took seven years (Deccan wars page). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The Timurid battle order of vanguard, centre, wings and reserve was kept, with the emperor or prince in the centre (Gommans). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: A news-writer network existed, but field intelligence and reaction were slow: after Nadir Shah crossed the Khyber 'it was two months before any decisive action was taken' (Karnal page). Middling-low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Low by evidence: Mughal armies broke when the commander vanished, before heavy losses. Samugarh 1658: after Rustam fell and Dara dismounted from his elephant, his 50,000-60,000 fled (Samugarh page); Karnal 1739: the imperial army was defeated within three hours (Karnal page). Contingents followed their mansabdar and habitually fell short of paper strength (Mansabdar page; Gommans). No battle gives a loss share at the break; 0.1 is a judgment. Rajput contingents fought to the death (Samugarh) but were a minority.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Mounted archers, matchlock infantry, an artillery park under its own commander outside the mansabdari system, war elephants and river fleets (Mughal Army page). Arms were assembled rather than integrated, so 0.6.
weightNotes.initiative: Mansabdars led their own contingents and princes ran whole campaigns, but loyalty was conditional and coordination poor (Gommans; Mansabdar page). Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The camp-city carried its own markets and was fed by banjara grain carriers (Gommans), letting it sustain sieges for years; the cost was slowness, and the Deccan war of 1681-1707 ran far beyond what revenue could support. Moderately high.

summary: An imperial army raised mainly through mansabdars, officers ranked by the number of horsemen they had to maintain and paid by revenue assignments (jagirs), with Turkic, Afghan, Persian and Rajput heavy horse archers at its core, a separately commanded artillery park, matchlock infantry, elephants and river fleets. Babur's founding victories combined a laager of chained carts and guns in the centre with flanking horse archers. Under Akbar and his successors war meant slow advances by a huge moving camp, sieges of hill forts and negotiated submissions, with battle as a last resort.
whyItWorked: Against Indian armies built around elephants and cavalry without gunpowder, the cart laager with guns and flanking horse archers was decisive (Panipat 1526: Ibrahim and 20,000 of his men killed; Khanwa 1527). Scale, money and siegecraft then let the empire reduce fortress after fortress (Chittor 1568) and co-opt defeated elites as mansabdars.
whereItFailed: Against mobile enemies who refused battle: the Marathas' roving bands outlasted Aurangzeb's 26-year Deccan war of sieges, and the Ahoms beat a Mughal river fleet at Saraighat (1671). Against a professional gunpowder army it collapsed: Nadir Shah destroyed the army at Karnal (1739) in three hours and sacked Delhi. Contingent loyalty made succession wars (Samugarh 1658) decide by defection.

sources.title: Gommans, Mughal Warfare: Indian Frontiers and High Roads to Empire 1500-1700 (Routledge, 2002)

name: Grande Armee corps system (1805-1812)

weightNotes.aggression: Napoleon sought the decisive battle against the main enemy army in every campaign 1805-1812 (Ulm, Austerlitz, Jena, Friedland, Wagram, Borodino); Chandler, Campaigns of Napoleon, parts 7-12.
weightNotes.maneuver: Manoeuvre sur les derrieres: Ulm 1805 forced Mack's surrender with little fighting, Jena 1806 placed the army across the Prussian line of retreat (Chandler parts 7-8). Kept below 1 because 1809-1812 battles (Aspern, Wagram, Borodino) became attritional slugging matches.
weightNotes.flanking: Corps marching on parallel routes converged on the enemy flank and rear (Davout at Auerstedt, Ney at Friedland, Davout's flank march at Austerlitz); Chandler parts 7-9.
weightNotes.siegePreference: The objective was the enemy field army, not fortresses; sieges (Danzig 1807, Saragossa 1808-09) were delegated to secondary forces. Capitals were taken after the field army was beaten (Vienna 1805, Berlin 1806).
weightNotes.reserveUse: Guard and Cavalry Reserve held back for the decisive blow (Austerlitz, Wagram); Napoleon's refusal to commit the Guard at Borodino shows the habit. Most corps strength was committed, so the held-back fraction is low-moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Light cavalry screens of each corps plus the Cavalry Reserve gave good operational intelligence in 1805; in 1806 Napoleon misplaced the main Prussian army (fought the smaller part at Jena), and in 1812 the cavalry wore out its horses early. Moderate-good.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Corps were built to hold an enemy army for a day until others arrived (Lannes at Saalfeld/Friedland, Davout at Auerstedt lost about a quarter of his corps and held); judgment from the Lannes thesis and Chandler, not a measured figure.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Each corps d'armee had infantry divisions, its own light cavalry, artillery and engineers and fought as a combined-arms unit (Everson, DTIC ADA284591). Grand batteries (Friedland, Wagram, Borodino) integrated artillery with assault.
weightNotes.initiative: Marshals ran their corps independently on the march and in the opening battle (ADA284591), but operational direction was entirely Napoleon's; marshals did poorly when left without him (Spain 1808-1812). Mid value.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Armies lived largely off the country and outran magazines; this worked in rich central Europe and failed in Poland 1807 and Russia 1812 (Jelinek, DTIC AD1022125).

summary: Napoleon split the army into permanent corps of 15,000-40,000 men, each a small army of all arms able to fight alone for a day. Corps marched dispersed on parallel roads within a day or two of each other ('march divided, fight united'), screened by light cavalry, and concentrated on the battlefield or on the enemy's line of communication. One corps fixed the enemy while others came in on the flank and rear; the Guard and Cavalry Reserve delivered or exploited the decisive blow, often after a grand battery had opened a gap. Supply relied on requisition and foraging plus short-lived depots, which bought speed. Conscription (Jourdan law 1798) fed replacements on a scale ancien-regime armies could not match.
whyItWorked: Dispersed marching gave speed and let the army feed itself, while each corps' ability to hold for a day meant concentration could happen on the battlefield itself. Opponents still marched as single slow armies tied to magazines and were outmanoeuvred before they could concentrate: Ulm 1805 captured an Austrian army with almost no battle, Jena-Auerstedt 1806 destroyed the Prussian field army in one day.
whereItFailed: Eylau 1807 (winter, poor roads and starving troops produced a bloody draw); Spain 1808-1812, where marshals without central direction and a guerrilla war defeated foraging logistics; Aspern-Essling 1809, a failed river crossing; Russia 1812, where foraging collapsed over vast poor country, horses and men died before Moscow, the Russians traded space and avoided encirclement, and Borodino became a frontal battle of attrition. The army of over 600,000 that crossed the Niemen came back with a small fraction.

sources.title: Everson, Marshal Jean Lannes in the Battles of Saalfeld, Pultusk, and Friedland 1806-1807 (CGSC thesis, DTIC ADA284591)
Jelinek, Napoleon's Logistics; or How Napoleon Learned to Worry about Supply (ACSC paper, DTIC AD1022125)
Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (Macmillan), parts 7-12
House, Towards Combined Arms Warfare (CSI Research Survey 2, 1984), chapter 1

name: European NATO middle powers (2026), e.g. Spain

weightNotes.aggression: Expeditionary forces built for coalition crisis management and NATO deterrence (Spain in NATO report 2026: eastern-flank deployments, Slovakia brigade), not for initiating war; national politics are casualty-averse (Spain left Iraq in 2004). Middling-low.
weightNotes.maneuver: Trained to NATO manoeuvre doctrine (AJP-01 lineage of AirLand Battle) with professional mechanised brigades; would fight manoeuvre if they had mass, but lack depth to sustain it.
weightNotes.flanking: Same NATO manoeuvre training; middling because brigades are few and would fight inside a US- or multinational-led corps plan.
weightNotes.siegePreference: No doctrinal interest in reducing cities; urban operations only as part of stabilisation (Afghanistan, Iraq, Lebanon UNIFIL). Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Small armies with little depth: forces deployed forward on the eastern flank are a large share of what is ready; reserves exist mostly as low-readiness units. Educated guess.
weightNotes.scouting: Good organic ISR for their size, but RAND's Libya study (RR-676) shows European air campaigns relied on US ISR, tankers and targeting; capped at 0.6 to reflect that dependence.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Low tolerance for casualties in public and political opinion (Spain withdrew its Iraq contingent after the 2004 Madrid bombings); formations would be preserved early. Below modern breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Professional all-arms brigades and joint training in NATO exercises; Spain fields an expeditionary amphibious group (Dedalo). Below the US because organic deep fires, air defence and EW are thin.
weightNotes.initiative: Long-service professional NCOs and officers trained in NATO mission command; Heritage (2025) calls the Spanish military 'professional and competent' despite underfunding.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: RUSI Preliminary Lessons (2022): 'no country in NATO, other than the US, has sufficient initial weapons stocks for warfighting'; with small munition stocks these forces must stay strictly inside supply and alliance logistics. High discipline by necessity.

summary: Small, all-volunteer, professional joint forces optimised since the 1990s for expeditionary coalition operations (Balkans, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Mali, UNIFIL) and, since 2022, for forward deterrence on NATO's eastern flank. They fight within a NATO or US-led command structure, with modern but few platforms, good training and NATO procedures, and limited stocks, ISR and long-range fires. Spain is typical: about 2% of GDP on defence in 2026, an amphibious/carrier group, Eurofighters with stand-off missiles, and battlegroups deployed to Latvia and Slovakia.
whyItWorked: Interoperability and professionalism make them effective contributors in coalitions: the 2011 Libya air campaign was carried largely by European aircraft (RAND RR-676), and multinational battlegroups provide credible tripwire deterrence. Quality of training and equipment is high per unit.
whereItFailed: Alone they cannot fight a high-intensity war: in Libya 2011 the European-led air campaign relied on air refuelling, suppression of air defences and ISR that the United States 'predominantly contributed' (RAND RR-676); RUSI judges no European ally has the stocks or industrial capacity for sustained warfighting. Afghanistan 2001-2021 and Mali 2013-2022 ended in withdrawal without achieving their political goals, and national caveats limited what contingents could do.

sources.title: Government of Spain, Spain in NATO: An ally that delivers and leads with principles (July 2026)
RAND, Precision and Purpose: Airpower in the Libyan Civil War (RR-676)
RUSI, Preliminary Lessons in Conventional Warfighting from Russia's Invasion of Ukraine: February-July 2022
Heritage Foundation Issue Brief 5393, Spain's Socialist Government Has the Least Responsible Security Policies in NATO (2025)

name: Ottoman classical army: janissaries and timariot sipahis (1450-1683)

weightNotes.aggression: Sultan-led campaigns almost every year of the classical period: Constantinople 1453, Chaldiran 1514, Mohacs 1526, Vienna 1529 and 1683 (Agoston, Last Muslim Conquest; battle pages). The army usually forced the enemy to attack prepared positions, so tactically less aggressive than strategically.
weightNotes.maneuver: Armies of 60,000-100,000 with 300 guns (Mohacs page) moved slowly along prepared roads; manoeuvre was by akinci raiders and the cavalry wings, not the main body (Murphey, Ottoman Warfare). Middling-low.
weightNotes.flanking: Battle plans used the cavalry wings against the enemy flanks: Anatolian cavalry ambushed the crusader flank at Varna (1444); at Mohacs the Ottomans 'launched a counterattack with cavalry and light infantry from both wings' (Varna, Mohacs pages).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Campaign objectives were fortresses: Constantinople (1453), Rhodes (1522), Belgrade (1521), Szigetvar (1566), Vienna (1529, 1683). Heavy artillery and sapping were core skills (Agoston, Guns for the Sultan). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The sultan's household troops, janissaries and artillery, stood in the centre behind carts and ditches while provincial cavalry fought on the wings; the janissaries were the last-line reserve that stopped Wladyslaw's charge at Varna (Varna page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Akinci light horse screened and raided ahead, and pre-war intelligence was good; but at Vienna 1683 Kara Mustafa failed to prepare for the relief army and left the rear to the Crimean Tatars (Vienna page). Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Vienna 1683: an Ottoman list records 48,544 casualties by 10 September out of an army Sakul estimates at about 120,000 (about 40%, siege attrition included) before the army broke under the relief army's charge on 12 September (Vienna page). The janissary centre was not broken in the victories at Varna 1444, Chaldiran 1514 and Mohacs 1526 (battle pages). Saint Gotthard 1664: losses fell 'mostly on the elite corps', no share given. The timariot cavalry broke contact earlier, with no figure. 0.3.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Artillery, musket-armed janissaries behind a cart barrier, sipahi lancer-archers on the wings and akinci raiders (Chaldiran: 'heavy artillery and thousands of Janissaries equipped with gunpowder weapons behind a barrier of carts'; Agoston). Among the most integrated armies of the 16th century.
weightNotes.initiative: Highly centralised under the sultan or grand vizier, with the Rumelian and Anatolian provincial contingents on the wings to a set plan (Varna page; Murphey). Little evidence of subordinate latitude.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Stockpiles and road stations prepared before each campaign (Vienna 1683: roads and bridges repaired and ammunition forwarded in advance, Vienna page); an army of 60,000 men and 40,000 horses needed half a million kg of food per day (Military of the Ottoman Empire page). Campaigns ended with the season (Murphey). High.

summary: A two-part army: the sultan's salaried household (janissary musketeers, artillery corps, household cavalry) and the far larger provincial cavalry of timariot sipahis, lancer-archers paid by land grants, plus akinci raiders and auxiliaries. In battle the janissaries and guns stood behind chained carts and ditches in the centre (the tabur), the provincial cavalry fought on the wings and drew the enemy onto the guns, and the household reserve finished the fight. Campaigns were prepared a year ahead with stockpiles and road stations and aimed at a key fortress, taken by artillery and mining.
whyItWorked: Scale, logistics and firepower: no European state could field 300 guns and a standing musket infantry in the 16th century (Mohacs page; Agoston). The tabur defence turned the enemy's attack into a killing ground (Chaldiran 1514 against Safavid cavalry without guns; Mohacs 1526, Hungarian lines collapsed within two hours). Siege artillery and engineers took Constantinople, Belgrade and Rhodes.
whereItFailed: Distance and season: Vienna in 1529 and 1683 lay at the end of the campaign radius; in 1683 a two-month siege left the army weak and demoralised and the relief army's cavalry routed it in under three hours. Western armies that held firm against the cavalry and out-fired the janissaries won (Saint Gotthard 1664 under Montecuccoli). By the 17th century timar cavalry was declining and the janissaries were politicised.

sources.title: Military of the Ottoman Empire, Wikipedia
Agoston, Guns for the Sultan (Cambridge UP, 2005)
Agoston, The Last Muslim Conquest (Princeton UP, 2021)

name: People's Army of Vietnam: people's war in the South (1965-1975)

weightNotes.aggression: Strategic offensives in 1968 (Tet), 1972 (Easter Offensive, 14 divisions and 26 independent regiments) and 1975, but between them main-force units fought only when they chose and withdrew to Laos and Cambodia (Tet, Easter Offensive pages; Pike, PAVN). Moderately high.
weightNotes.maneuver: 1975 was a manoeuvre campaign: Buon Ma Thuot taken on 18 March by a thrust from Cambodia, then forces moved over 350 miles south to Saigon by 30 April (1975 spring offensive page). Earlier, ambush and withdrawal rather than manoeuvre for decision.
weightNotes.flanking: Ambushes and close attacks on landing zones (Ia Drang 1965, where an ambushed US battalion suffered 'a casualty rate of over 50%'); in 1972 assaults were mostly frontal and poorly coordinated (Ia Drang, Easter Offensive pages). Middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Sieges were used to fix and draw in the enemy: Khe Sanh besieged five months in 1968, An Loc in 1972 (Khe Sanh, Easter Offensive pages). Field forces, not towns, were the usual target until 1975. Middling-low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Echeloned forces and strategic reserves held in the North and the sanctuaries; in 1975 the reserve corps were committed only once the ARVN cracked (1975 spring offensive page; Victory in Vietnam, official history). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Detailed reconnaissance and rehearsal before attacks, sapper units, and intelligence from the southern population (People's Army of Vietnam page; Elliott, The Vietnamese War). High.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Easter Offensive 1972: 14 divisions and 26 independent regiments kept attacking and holding (Quang Tri citadel until September) while taking about 100,000 casualties (Easter Offensive page), roughly half the committed force if a division is about 10,000 men (assumption, not on the page). Hue 1968: held the Citadel a little over a month, 1,042-5,133 killed, force size not given (Hue page). Main-force units also broke contact and withdrew when losses mounted (Ia Drang 1965, Dak To 1967), no shares recorded. 0.35, partly derived.
weightNotes.combinedArms: By 1972 tanks (T-54, PT-76), 130 mm guns and SA-7s were fielded, but 'failure of tactical coordination was one of PAVN's prime weaknesses' and almost all armour committed was lost (Easter Offensive page). Better in 1975. 0.45.
weightNotes.initiative: Party control through commissars and front commands, with detailed set-piece plans; regional fronts (B2, Tri-Thien) had latitude, but units executed rehearsed plans rather than improvising (Pike, PAVN; Victory in Vietnam). Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Offensives were timed to stockpiles moved down the Ho Chi Minh Trail by the 559th Group's binh tram stations and trucks (Ho Chi Minh Trail page); the 1972 offensive was 'hampered by high casualties, lack of fuel' when it outran supply (Easter Offensive page). High.

summary: A party-led regular army fighting alongside Viet Cong regional and guerrilla forces under the people's war doctrine: protracted war, with guerrilla, regional and main forces each doing their part, and main-force units committed to conventional offensives when the balance allowed. In the South its regiments and divisions operated from bunker complexes and sanctuaries in Laos and Cambodia, fought close to negate US firepower, and withdrew when losses mounted. Everything was supplied down the Ho Chi Minh Trail. From 1972 it became a conventional combined-arms force with armour, heavy artillery and SAMs.
whyItWorked: Political aims governed military ones: Tet (1968) was a military defeat but turned US opinion and led to negotiations. The trail sustained the war through years of bombing, sanctuaries let units rebuild, and close-in tactics blunted US air and artillery. In 1975 a well-prepared offensive against an ARVN without US air support broke the South between the fall of Buon Ma Thuot (18 March) and Saigon (30 April).
whereItFailed: When it fought conventionally against massed US firepower it lost heavily: the Tet offensive's urban assaults were repelled with very heavy losses and no uprising; the 1972 Easter Offensive cost about 100,000 casualties and almost all its armour (134 T-54s, 56 PT-76s and 60 T-34s) to air power and poor infantry-armour coordination. Khe Sanh (1968) absorbed over 114,000 tons of bombs in three months.

sources.title: Pike, PAVN: People's Army of Vietnam (Presidio, 1986)
Elliott, The Vietnamese War: Revolution and Social Change in the Mekong Delta (M.E. Sharpe, 2003)
Military History Institute of Vietnam, Victory in Vietnam, tr. Pribbenow (UP of Kansas, 2002)

name: PLA informatized/intelligentized joint operations (2026)

weightNotes.aggression: Strategic 'active defence' but operationally offensive: Science of Military Strategy (2013) and the DoD 2024 report describe seizing the initiative early with massed long-range joint fires (JOINT SWORD 2023 rehearsed this). Tempered because the political leadership has preferred coercion short of war since 1979.
weightNotes.maneuver: Systems destruction warfare (RAND RR-1708; DoD 2024: 'principal theory guiding its way of war') aims to paralyse the enemy's operational system by striking nodes rather than annihilating forces, which is manoeuvrist in intent; held near the middle because ground manoeuvre at scale is untested since 1979.
weightNotes.flanking: Doctrine favours striking key vulnerabilities across domains (Multi-Domain Precision Warfare) rather than frontal battle, but there is no recent evidence of operational-level envelopment; middling, educated judgement.
weightNotes.siegePreference: The defining contingency (Taiwan) ends in seizing ports, airfields and cities; DoD 2024 notes the PLA has 'not yet demonstrated' the urban warfare it would need. Raised above Western profiles for that objective set.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Echeloned joint campaign phases (firepower strike, blockade, landing) imply follow-on forces and a large strategic reserve inland; 0.35 is an educated guess.
weightNotes.scouting: Large reconnaissance satellite constellation, over-the-horizon radar, drones and the space/cyber/EW force created in 2015 (RAND RR-2058 on the Strategic Support Force) built to find and target US forces at range; below US because the kill chain beyond the first island chain is unproven.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: No combat since 1979 (Sino-Vietnamese War, where the PLA accepted heavy losses: Zhang, Deng Xiaoping's Long War); political-work system aims at high cohesion. Educated guess, kept below modern breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: 2015-17 reforms created combined arms brigades and theatre joint commands, and the 2020 Joint Operations Outline (Trial) pushes jointness to tactical level (DoD 2024). DoD also notes operational regulations last updated in 1999, so integration is still maturing.
weightNotes.initiative: DoD 2024 cites the 'Five Incapables' slogan: officers who cannot judge situations, understand intent, make decisions, deploy troops or handle the unexpected. Party committee command and centralised C2 keep this low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Joint Logistic Support Force and civil mobilisation (ro-ro ferries) are planned, but DoD 2024 states long-distance logistics at the scale of a Taiwan campaign is undemonstrated; operations would likely stay tied to the coast and strike range.

summary: A large, rapidly modernised force whose doctrine treats war as a confrontation between operational systems. It plans to open with massed precision strikes by the Rocket Force, air force and navy against command, ISR, air bases and logistics (systems destruction warfare, now Multi-Domain Precision Warfare), contest space and the electromagnetic spectrum, and keep US forces outside the first island chain with layered anti-access/area-denial (missiles, submarines, aviation). Ground and amphibious forces then exploit the paralysis. Command is centralised through theatre joint commands under the Central Military Commission.
whyItWorked: Not tested in combat. On paper the A2/AD complex is strong: CSIS's 24-run Taiwan wargame cost the US and its allies dozens of ships, hundreds of aircraft and tens of thousands of servicemembers. The PLA has the world's largest navy, a deep precision-missile inventory and industrial capacity to replace losses.
whereItFailed: Last real test, Vietnam 1979, exposed poor logistics, communications and combined arms and heavy casualties for limited gains (Zhang 2015). In CSIS's 2023 wargames a conventional amphibious invasion of Taiwan was defeated in most of the 24 runs, with China also losing heavily. DoD 2024 flags command initiative and urban/long-distance logistics as unproven, and senior purges may have disrupted readiness.

sources.title: DoD, Military and Security Developments Involving the PRC 2024 (Annual Report to Congress)
Engstrom, Systems Confrontation and System Destruction Warfare (RAND RR-1708, 2018)
CASI translation, PLA Science of Military Strategy (2013)
RAND, The Creation of the PLA Strategic Support Force (RR-2058)
CSIS, The First Battle of the Next War: Wargaming a Chinese Invasion of Taiwan (2023)
Zhang Xiaoming, Deng Xiaoping's Long War: The Military Conflict between China and Vietnam, 1979-1991 (UNC Press, 2015)

name: Prussian army of Frederick II (1740-1763)

weightNotes.aggression: Frederick: 'I prefer the boldness of a general who would rather hazard a battle at the right time', and a purely defensive plan 'is useless' (General Principles of War, 1748/1753). He attacked larger armies repeatedly: Leuthen 33,000 against 66,000 (Leuthen page), Zorndorf, Kunersdorf, Torgau.
weightNotes.maneuver: Interior lines and fast marches: 274 km in 12 days before Leuthen (Leuthen page); Rossbach followed five days of manoeuvre (Rossbach page). Battles themselves were bloody and attritional, so not higher (Showalter).
weightNotes.flanking: The oblique order refused one wing and massed against the enemy's flank (Oblique order page); Leuthen's approach was screened behind low hills to hit the Austrian left; Seydlitz's cavalry decided Rossbach from the flank.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Frederick sought decision in the field; the siege of Prague was abandoned after Kolin (Kolin page), and siege warfare was a Prussian weakness (Duffy). Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Nearly everything was committed to the attack; at Kunersdorf the king fed exhausted battalions into repeated assaults until the army dissolved (Kunersdorf page). Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Hussar patrols mainly guarded against desertion (General Principles), and Daun achieved complete surprise with a pre-dawn attack at Hochkirch (Hochkirch page). Peacetime knowledge of the Silesian ground helped at Leuthen. Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Kolin 1757: 13,733 of 34,000 lost (40%) before withdrawing (Kolin page). Hochkirch 1758: over 30% lost in a surprise attack and the army still withdrew in order (Hochkirch page). Torgau 1760: 16,670 lost (about a third) in a victory (Torgau page). Kunersdorf 1759: the army dissolved and only 3,000 of 48,000 stayed with the king that night (Kunersdorf page). Frederick: wounded officers and men 'would not leave their posts' (General Principles). 0.35.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Superb infantry fire and the cavalry under Seydlitz as a shock arm (Rossbach, Zorndorf), with heavy guns added after 1757 (167 cannon at Leuthen). The arms fought in sequence more than in mutual support. Middling.
weightNotes.initiative: Frederick: 'everything that happens is the work of a single person' and 'no one talks, but all act, and the command of the general is promptly followed' (General Principles). Seydlitz's independent charges are the exception. Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Magazine-based: troops must 'want for nothing, be it meat, bread, straw', one can undertake everything 'if one only has enough food', and 'all wars in which we move too far from our borders are useless' (General Principles). High.

summary: A drilled long-service army, half native cantonists and half foreign recruits held together by severe discipline, fighting in thin lines with the fastest musketry in Europe. Frederick sought short, decisive campaigns on interior lines: quick marches, an attack on the enemy flank in oblique order with one wing refused, and heavy cavalry under Seydlitz to finish. Operations were tied to magazines close to the frontiers, and command was centralised in the king.
whyItWorked: Drill gave manoeuvre speed and fire rate no opponent matched, so a smaller Prussian army could concentrate on one enemy flank: Rossbach (1757, 22,000 beat 41,000 in about 90 minutes) and Leuthen (1757, 33,000 beat 66,000). Interior lines let Prussia fight Austria, Russia and France in turn, and the army's ability to absorb 30-40% losses and re-form kept it in the war for seven years.
whereItFailed: Against larger, well-led armies that held strong positions or attacked first, the costs were ruinous: Kolin (1757, 40% lost), Hochkirch (1758, surprised at night), Kunersdorf (1759, the army temporarily dissolved). Centralised command meant detached corps under lesser generals were destroyed. By 1760-62 Prussia survived on attrition and the collapse of the enemy coalition, not on battlefield decision.

sources.title: Frederick II, General Principles of War (1748/1753), German History in Documents and Images
Showalter, The Wars of Frederick the Great (Longman, 1996)
Duffy, The Army of Frederick the Great (Emperor's Press, 1996)

name: Qing Eight Banners and Green Standard army (1644-1799)

weightNotes.aggression: Conquest of Ming China (1644-83), the Dzungar wars and the Ten Great Campaigns of the 18th century, including four invasions of Burma (Eight Banners, Dzungar-Qing Wars, Sino-Burmese War pages). High.
weightNotes.maneuver: Manchu and Mongol banner cavalry could move fast (Shanhai Pass 1644 opened the road to Beijing), but the great steppe campaigns were slow logistical operations (Kangxi's 80-day trek across the Gobi in 1696, Jao Modo page). Middling.
weightNotes.flanking: Standard order put cannon and infantry in the centre and Manchu and Mongol cavalry on the flanks (Jao Modo page). No distinctive envelopment doctrine in the sources used. Middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Han Banner artillery decided the siege of Dalinghe (1631) and cannon were carried on camelback into the steppe (Eight Banners, Jao Modo pages); but the decisive objective in the Dzungar wars was the enemy field army. Balanced.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Banners were held as an emergency force behind the Green Standard garrisons, which 'actively military governed China locally' while bannermen 'were only brought into emergency situations' (Green Standard Army page). Moderate, educated guess at battle level.
weightNotes.scouting: Mongol allies and steppe intelligence served well against the Dzungars, but in Burma the army walked into the Bhamo-Kaungton trap and was encircled at Maymyo (Sino-Burmese War page). Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Banner troops held until destroyed: Maymyo 1768, the encircled bannerman army fought three days and only 2,500 of 30,000 survived, as prisoners, about 92% lost (Sino-Burmese War page); Zhenjiang 1842, the 1,583 Manchu bannermen fought until overrun and then committed mass suicide (Zhenjiang page). Jao Modo 1696: the Qing centre 'began to collapse' but held and won (Jao Modo page). The Green Standard broke earlier, no figure. 0.6 for the banner core.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Manchu and Mongol mounted archers, Han Banner artillery and musketeers, and Green Standard infantry; at Jao Modo the Qing 'bombarded Dzungar troops with their cannons and then advanced behind a wooden barricade' with cavalry on the flanks (Jao Modo page).
weightNotes.initiative: Campaigns were directed by the emperor through palace memorials (Kangxi led in person in 1696); banner commanders had little latitude and failure was punished (Elliott, Manchu Way; Sino-Burmese War page). Low-middling.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Kangxi's 1696 expedition was preceded by 1,333 grain carts (Dzungar-Qing Wars page) and Perdue (China Marches West) shows that the state's logistical capacity is what finally beat the Dzungars. Burma was lost to disease and supply, not tactics. High.

summary: A hereditary military caste of Manchu, Mongol and Han bannermen, stipended and garrisoned, formed the elite strike force; the far larger Green Standard Army of former Ming troops garrisoned and policed the provinces. Banner cavalry kept Manchu mounted archery while Han bannermen manned artillery cast with Jesuit and defector help. The great campaigns against the Dzungars were won by logistics: grain convoys, depots and cannon carried across the Gobi, with the emperor directing from the capital or the field.
whyItWorked: The Qing fused steppe cavalry with Chinese artillery and the fiscal resources of China. That combination took Beijing after Shanhai Pass (1644), broke Galdan's army at Jao Modo (1696, Dzungar army 'bereft of artillery' broke under cannon and musket fire), and by the 1750s destroyed the Dzungar state and incorporated Xinjiang and Tibet.
whereItFailed: Outside the steppe and north China climate: the Burma invasions (1765-69) cost over 70,000 Qing soldiers, mostly to disease, and the main banner army was annihilated at Maymyo (1768). After the Ten Great Campaigns banner quality declined, and against an industrial navy the system failed entirely (First Opium War, Zhenjiang 1842).

sources.title: Perdue, China Marches West: The Qing Conquest of Central Eurasia (Harvard UP, 2005)
Elliott, The Manchu Way: The Eight Banners and Ethnic Identity in Late Imperial China (Stanford UP, 2001)
Graff and Higham (eds.), A Military History of China (UP of Kentucky, 2012)

name: Roman army of the Principate

weightNotes.aggression: Goldsworthy (Roman Army at War) stresses the Roman drive to seek battle and win moral dominance; Agricola marched into Caledonia to force Mons Graupius (AD 83). Not 0.9 because frontier policy after Augustus was often containment.
weightNotes.maneuver: Roman battles were won by sustained, methodical infantry pressure and line relief rather than operational manoeuvre (Sabin 2000, Face of Roman Battle); attrition-leaning.
weightNotes.flanking: Auxiliary cavalry on the wings (Mons Graupius: 3,000 cavalry on the flanks per Tacitus) gave a flanking arm, but the decisive arm was frontal infantry.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Conquest was consolidated by systematic sieges: Jerusalem 70, Masada 73/74 (circumvallation and a ramp of about half a million tons of earth), Dacian fortresses 105/106. Field battle still preferred when the enemy offered it.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Tactically the Romans kept strong reserves (Mons Graupius: legions held in reserve in front of the camp while auxilia fought). Strategically the Principate had almost no central reserve, legions sat on the frontiers; 0.35 splits the two.
weightNotes.scouting: Exploratores and speculatores existed, but Teutoburg (AD 9) shows a column marching into an ambush on false intelligence; middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Highest of the ancient profiles: drill, line relief and fortified camps let Roman units fall back and reform (Sabin 2000; Goldsworthy). Kept at 0.12 so it stays below the low end (~0.1-0.3) of ancient breakpoints once cohesion shifts them up.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Legionary heavy infantry with auxiliary cavalry, archers and slingers, field artillery and engineers in one force (Auxilia article; Roman military engineering); Arrian's order against the Alans (AD 135) mixes all four.
weightNotes.initiative: Centurions and legates had local latitude and provincial governors waged war on their own authority, but battle plans were set by the commander; moderate.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Roth (Logistics of the Roman Army at War) documents granaries, river and sea supply, and the nightly fortified marching camp (Castra article); Romans rarely outran supply.

summary: A long-service professional army of citizen legions (heavy infantry with pilum and gladius) and non-citizen auxilia (cavalry, archers, light and line infantry). On campaign it built a fortified marching camp every night, moved on a supplied road and river network, and fought set-piece battles with auxilia in front or on the wings and legions as the decisive line or reserve. Wars of conquest ended in methodical siege and engineering: circumvallation, ramps, artillery and rams.
whyItWorked: Training, discipline and standardisation let units relieve each other in line and absorb losses that broke citizen and tribal armies. Engineering and logistics let it keep the field year-round, besiege anything and never be caught unfortified at night. Long service gave a deep bench of experienced centurions.
whereItFailed: On the march through forest against an enemy it did not see: Teutoburg (AD 9), three legions lost to Arminius's ambush. Against mobile horse-archer armies on open ground it could not close: Carrhae (53 BC, late Republic, horse archers resupplied by a 1,000-camel train and feigned retreats drawing off Publius Crassus) set the pattern that recurred on the Parthian frontier. Frontier dispersion meant a disaster could not be quickly replaced.

name: Russian Armed Forces as observed in Ukraine (2022-2026)

weightNotes.aggression: Continuous offensive pressure from 2023 through 2025 despite very high losses (RUSI Meatgrinder 2023; RUSI Third Year 2025: 'highly attritional', both sides seeking to inflict maximum damage). Not higher because Russia spent mid-2022 to late 2023 on the defensive behind prepared lines.
weightNotes.maneuver: The 2022 manoeuvre plan (10-day seizure of Kyiv, RUSI Preliminary Lessons) failed and was abandoned; since then armour is 'rarely used for attempts at breakthrough' and is used as fire support (RUSI Meatgrinder). Strongly attritional.
weightNotes.flanking: Later offensives (Avdiivka 2023-24, Pokrovsk axis 2024-25) worked by slow pincers around towns rather than frontal assault on the strongest point, but at tactical depth only; low-middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Campaign shaped as the reduction of fortified towns one at a time: Mariupol 2022, Sievierodonetsk/Lysychansk 2022, Bakhmut 2022-23, Avdiivka 2024, under artillery and glide-bomb (FAB-500 with UMPK kits, RUSI Meatgrinder) bombardment.
weightNotes.reserveUse: RUSI Preliminary Lessons: the 2022 plan had 'no reversionary courses of action' and reserves were thin; later mobilisation (2022) and contract recruiting fed rotations, but forces are committed piecemeal to sustain pressure. Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Poor in 2022 (culturally vulnerable to deception, RUSI). By 2023 Orlan-10 and other UAVs were tightly tied to fires through the Strelets system (RUSI Meatgrinder), and drone reconnaissance is now pervasive. Middling-high.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: RUSI Preliminary Lessons: 'a culture of reinforcing failure unless orders are changed at higher levels'; disposable assault infantry absorbs very uneven casualties (Meatgrinder). Yet the Kyiv (March 2022) and Kherson (November 2022) withdrawals were orderly. High tolerance, held at 0.3 so it stays below modern breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: RUSI Preliminary Lessons: capabilities that should magnify one another 'must be employed sequentially', fratricide and poor EW deconfliction, land component dominant over air. BTGs failed as combined arms units and were replaced by functional infantry groupings (Meatgrinder). Partly improved reconnaissance-strike complex keeps it above 0.3.
weightNotes.initiative: RUSI Preliminary Lessons: culturally averse to giving subordinates context to exercise judgement, dishonest reporting culture, weak junior leadership. Adaptation is centralised and reactive (Meatgrinder).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Rail-bound logistics: the 2022 Kyiv axis outran its supply (stalled columns) and GMLRS strikes destroyed depots in July 2022; afterwards headquarters and depots were pulled back out of range and operations stayed close to railheads (RUSI Meatgrinder). Averaged across the war.

summary: An artillery-centric force that fights attritional battles. After the failed 2022 coup-de-main on Kyiv it reorganised from Battalion Tactical Groups into functional groupings: disposable and assault infantry probe and skirmish to locate Ukrainian positions, which are then destroyed by artillery, mortars, glide bombs and FPV drones cued by Orlan-type UAVs; armour gives fire support rather than breakthrough. On defence it builds deep engineered belts (minefields, ditches, concrete trenches) backed by dense electronic warfare. Strategically it runs a missile and drone campaign against Ukraine's energy grid and cities.
whyItWorked: Mass and firepower: in June 2022 Russia had about a 10:1 advantage in volume of fire (RUSI Preliminary Lessons). Engineering and minefields defeated Ukraine's 2023 counteroffensive (RUSI Stormbreak: deliberate assaults advanced only 700-1,200 m every five days). Russia adapts centrally and fast enough on recurring problems (thermal camouflage, EW against drones, glide bombs) and has mobilised industry and manpower to sustain a war of attrition.
whereItFailed: Kyiv 2022: a 12:1 force ratio north of the capital (RUSI) could not overcome poor tactical competence, no fallback plan, and Ukrainian artillery; the force withdrew in early April. Kharkiv (September 2022) and Kherson (November 2022) showed it could be outmanoeuvred when pinned and its supply interdicted. Gains since 2023 have come at very high casualty cost per km, and RUSI judges Russian units lose coordination quickly in dynamic situations.

name: Sengoku-period daimyo armies (1467-1615)

weightNotes.aggression: A century of endemic war between daimyo; Nobunaga's attack on Imagawa's camp at Okehazama (1560) and Hideyoshi's invasion of Korea (1592, 158,800 prepared across nine divisions) show the offensive habit (Okehazama, Korea invasion pages). High.
weightNotes.maneuver: Surprise and speed won Okehazama, and in Korea Konishi reached Hanseong on 10 June 1592, 18 days after landing at Busan (Korea invasion page). But much campaigning was castle-to-castle. Middling.
weightNotes.flanking: Encirclement occurred (Mikatagahara 1573: the Tokugawa-Oda force 'almost totally annihilated... after being encircled'), but most set battles were frontal clashes of retainer bands. Middling.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Castle warfare dominated: Odawara (1590) was a starvation siege, Takamatsu (1582) was flooded by diverting a river with dikes, Nagashino (1575) began as a siege (Odawara, Takamatsu, Nagashino pages). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Daimyo kept their own bodyguard (hatamoto) in hand; little evidence of a doctrinal reserve. Educated guess, low-middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Nobunaga found and struck Yoshimoto's camp at Okehazama; Takeda's vassals warned Katsuyori of Oda's arrival before Nagashino (Okehazama, Nagashino pages). Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Retainer bands held very long: Nagashino 1575, the Takeda charged repeatedly and retreated only after losing about 10,000 of 15,000 (two-thirds, Shincho Koki chronicle figure incl. pursuit, Nagashino page); Sekigahara 1600, the Shimazu contingent broke out of encirclement with 200 men left; Mikatagahara 1573, the encircled Tokugawa-Oda force was 'almost totally annihilated'. But army-level collapse came from defection or loss of the lord at low losses (Sekigahara, Okehazama), with no share recorded. 0.4 splits the two.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Ashigaru with arquebus, spear and bow in specialised units around mounted and foot samurai; at Nagashino Oda guns fought behind horse fences (the classic '3,000 guns in three ranks' is disputed; Nagashino, Ashigaru pages). 0.7.
weightNotes.initiative: Daimyo and their senior vassals commanded semi-independent contingents; the Sengoku period saw 'many instances of vassals rebelling against their lords' (Sengoku period page). High latitude, but unreliable.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Domestic campaigns were short and local; Hideyoshi kept a huge army supplied for a months-long starvation siege at Odawara, but in Korea the Joseon navy's attacks on supply fleets 'forced the Japanese forces to withdraw from the northern provinces' (Korea invasion page). Middling.

summary: Armies of regional warlords built from samurai retainer bands and increasingly from drilled ashigaru foot soldiers organised by weapon: arquebus (from 1543), long spear and bow, with mounted samurai as shock troops. Campaigns turned on castles, taken by starvation, mining or flooding, and on set battles often decided by surprise, the death of a commander, or defection of allies. Unification under Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu brought very large, well-supplied armies, field fortifications and massed firearms.
whyItWorked: Rapid adoption of firearms and specialised infantry units, combined with field works, let disciplined armies defeat brave but unsupported charges (Nagashino 1575). Leaders who struck fast at the enemy commander won out of proportion to numbers (Okehazama 1560). By 1592 Japan could ship and supply an army of about 150,000 and take the Korean capital in under three weeks.
whereItFailed: Cohesion rested on personal loyalty, so armies broke when the lord died (Okehazama) or allies changed sides (Sekigahara 1600). Overseas the system lacked naval control and logistics: Yi Sun-sin's fleet cut the supply line and Ming armies retook Pyongyang; by 1593 the invasion force was down from about 150,000 to 53,000, and the war ended with withdrawal in 1598.

sources.title: Conlan, State of War: The Violent Order of Fourteenth-Century Japan (2003)

name: Red Army deep operations (1941-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: Offensive doctrine in both periods: in 1941 pre-war plans and Directive No. 3 ordered immediate counterattacks (Dubno-Brody, Smolensk) that failed; 1943-45 a continuous series of front-level offensives (Glantz, Great Patriotic War and Maturation of Soviet Operational Art, DTIC ADA194152). Same value for 1941 and 1945.
weightNotes.maneuver: Mature 1944-45 value about 0.8: tank armies exploited 150 km+ into the depth (Bagration, Vistula-Oder; Glantz ADA194152). 1941-42 value about 0.3: mechanised corps shattered, tanks used in small infantry-support brigades (House ch. 4). Set between, leaning to the mature state; the snapshot's command and training ratings carry the 1941 collapse.
weightNotes.flanking: Double envelopments became the signature of 1942-45 (Uranus at Stalingrad, Korsun, Bagration, Iasi-Kishinev). In 1941 commanders deployed evenly along the front 'as if on a textbook exercise' (House ch. 4), so the 1941 value would be about 0.3.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Objectives were enemy groupings; cities were stormed late in the war (Budapest, Konigsberg, Berlin) when they blocked the axis. Low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Stavka held strategic reserve armies and fed them in at the decisive moment (Moscow December 1941, Stalingrad November 1942, Steppe Front at Kursk 1943); deep echelonment was central to deep battle theory (Glantz).
weightNotes.scouting: 1941 near 0.2: surprise on 22 June and repeated encirclements. 1943-45 about 0.6: reconnaissance in force before offensives, partisans and maskirovka deception that concealed the main axis (Bagration). Middle value.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Order No. 227 ('Not a step back', July 1942) and tolerance of very high losses kept formations attacking or holding until exhausted; withdrawal came late. Judgment.
weightNotes.combinedArms: 1944-45 tank armies of tank and mechanised corps, artillery breakthrough corps and close air armies (House ch. 4; Glantz). 1941 value about 0.25: Stavka Circular No. 1 of 15 July 1941 stripped divisions of tanks and antitank units because commanders could not coordinate them (House ch. 4).
weightNotes.initiative: Highly centralised in both periods: Stavka directives and detailed army plans; junior initiative low, improving at front and army level in 1944-45. The 1937-38 purges had removed much of the officer corps (House ch. 4).
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: 1943-45 offensives paused to rebuild rail and supply between operations and culminated at about 300-500 km (Vistula, August 1944); Lend-Lease trucks carried the mobile forces (House ch. 4). 1941 value about 0.3.

summary: Soviet theory of the 1930s (Triandafillov, Tukhachevsky) called for simultaneous attack through the whole depth of the enemy defence: rifle armies and massed artillery break in, then mobile groups of tanks, motorised infantry and cavalry, supported by aviation and airborne drops, exploit deep to destroy reserves and encircle. The purges and a botched 1940-41 reorganisation meant that on 22 June 1941 the Red Army was caught mid-transition; its mechanised corps were destroyed and whole fronts encircled. It survived on mass mobilisation, scorched earth, the evacuation of industry and strategic reserves, then rebuilt from 1942: tank corps, then from January 1943 coherent tank armies, artillery breakthrough divisions, deception and deep echelonment. By 1944-45 it ran successive front offensives of 150-500 km against a thinly stretched Wehrmacht.
whyItWorked: Once rebuilt, deep operations matched the Soviet strengths (mass, artillery production, T-34s, Lend-Lease trucks) against a German army with no depth. Maskirovka hid the main blow (Bagration, June 1944, destroyed Army Group Centre), massed artillery broke the defence, and tank armies exploited before German reserves could react. Defensively, the deep belts at Kursk (July 1943) absorbed the last major German offensive in the east.
whereItFailed: 1941: Bialystok-Minsk, Kiev (the largest encirclement of the war) and Vyazma-Bryansk cost several million men, mostly prisoners, because the Red Army was untrained in its own doctrine and ordered into hopeless counterattacks. Finland 1939-40 showed it could not coordinate a deliberate attack. Kharkov, May 1942, an offensive that walked into encirclement; Operation Mars at Rzhev, November-December 1942, a costly failure; Third Kharkov, February-March 1943, after advancing beyond supply. Even successful operations cost far more men than the German defenders lost (Prokhorovka, the Seelow Heights).

name: Spanish Habsburg tercios and the Army of Flanders (1534-1643)

weightNotes.aggression: Offensive in Italy and Germany (Muhlberg 1547, Saint-Quentin 1557, Nordlingen 1634), but in the Low Countries Spain fought a war of position: 'Siege warfare, rather than set-piece battles, dominated the Eighty Years' War' (Army of Flanders page; Parker). Neutral.
weightNotes.maneuver: Deep pike-and-shot squares were slow, and in 1639 just under half of the 77,000-man army sat in 208 small garrisons (Army of Flanders page). Strategic movement along the Spanish Road was impressive but operations were attritional.
weightNotes.flanking: Sleeves of shot protected the squares, and squares could face every direction (Rocroi), but battle plans were frontal; Spanish cavalry was the weak arm: at Rocroi Gassion's horse routed the Spanish left and Enghien rode into the exposed flank (Rocroi page).
weightNotes.siegePreference: The Army of Flanders' war was trace italienne sieges: Ostend held out three years (1601-04) before falling (Ostend page); Parker's Military Revolution thesis is built on this theatre. High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Veteran Spanish tercios in front with mercenary infantry behind (Rocroi); at Nordlingen the commanders fed 'a constant stream of reinforcements' to the Albuch (Nordlingen page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: No distinctive reconnaissance practice is recorded in the sources used; at Rocroi Melo accepted battle before his reinforcements arrived, judging his army the stronger (Rocroi page). Educated guess, middling-low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Rocroi 1643: the Spanish tercios held, enveloped, until about half were dead and then surrendered on terms; Guthrie lists 3,400 killed and 2,000 captured of the five Spanish battalions, of 7,000 Spanish infantry about 1,776 escaped (Rocroi page), about 49% killed. The army as a whole (Melo: 6,000 casualties and 4,000 captured of 27,000, about 37%) broke earlier because German and Walloon units fled. Nordlingen 1634: the Albuch held against repeated assaults (Nordlingen page). 0.5.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Pioneered the integration of pike and arquebus (Cordoba's reforms; tercio of 8 pike and 2 arquebus companies in 1534, the shot ratio rising later; Tercio page). Cavalry and artillery support were weaker, so 0.6.
weightNotes.initiative: Tercios could 'divide into mobile units and even individual melee units without the loss of cohesion' (Tercio page) and detached companies garrisoned and skirmished on their own. But command at army level was fragmented and politicised.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The Spanish Road moved over 123,000 men from Italy to Flanders 1567-1620 through staging posts, and the army ran a military hospital (Spanish Road, Army of Flanders pages; Parker). Lowered because chronic pay arrears caused repeated mutinies and the sack of Antwerp (1576).

summary: Long-service volunteer infantry regiments (tercios) of pikemen and arquebusiers/musketeers, Spanish veterans stiffened by an officer corps of minor nobility, serving with Italian, Walloon and German contingents. They fought in deep pike squares surrounded by sleeves of shot, could split into smaller detachments, and held entrenched positions stubbornly. The Army of Flanders, supplied over the Spanish Road and by sea, spent most of its time besieging or garrisoning fortified towns.
whyItWorked: Training and a high proportion of veterans gave unmatched cohesion; the pike-and-shot combination beat Swiss pike and French gendarmes in the Italian Wars and dominated European infantry for a century. A logistic system spanning Italy, the Alps and the Low Countries kept a large army in the field for 80 years, and at Nordlingen (1634) the tercios on the Albuch broke the Swedish army.
whereItFailed: Money: the crown could not pay, and mutinies (the 1576 sack of Antwerp) cost whole campaigns. Deep squares were slow and vulnerable to the lighter, more firepower-heavy linear tactics and better cavalry of the Dutch, Swedes and French: at Rocroi (1643) the French horse routed the Spanish left, Enghien took the infantry in flank and rear, and massed artillery hammered the squares until they surrendered. The sieges of the Low Countries were slow and the Dutch were never subdued.

sources.title: Parker, The Army of Flanders and the Spanish Road 1567-1659 (Cambridge UP, 2004 ed.)
Parker, The Military Revolution (Cambridge UP, 1996 ed.)

name: Swedish army of Gustavus Adolphus (1618-1635)

weightNotes.aggression: Gustavus 'employed... very aggressive tactics, where attack was stressed over defense' (Gustavus Adolphus page): Breitenfeld 1631, the forced crossing of the Lech at Rain 1632, the failed assault on Wallenstein's entrenched Alte Veste and the attack at Lutzen 1632.
weightNotes.maneuver: The 1631-32 campaign carried the army from Pomerania to Bavaria and Rain was crossed under smoke and a prefabricated bridge (Rain page), but the war was also one of positional camps (Nuremberg/Alte Veste). Middling-high.
weightNotes.flanking: At Lutzen Gustavus 'swung round to outflank the Imperial left'; at Breitenfeld the second line was shifted to form a new front when the Saxons fled (Lutzen, Breitenfeld pages).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Sought field battle; fortified towns were taken by quick assault or negotiation. The direct attack on Wallenstein's entrenched camp failed with 2,500 casualties (Alte Veste page). Low-middling.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Two-line deployment with a real second line and reserve: at Breitenfeld 'reserves and Baner's units from the second line' reinforced the exposed flank (Breitenfeld page; Roberts, Gustavus Adolphus). Moderate-high for the era.
weightNotes.scouting: No distinctive reconnaissance record; Lutzen was fought in fog and the king himself rode into an enemy unit. Educated guess, middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Lutzen 1632: about 6,000 casualties of 19,000 (about 32%) and the army held the field and won after the king was killed, some brigades losing up to 65% (Lutzen page). Breitenfeld 1631: about 1,000 killed in the opening cannonade and the line re-formed after the Saxons fled (Breitenfeld page). Nordlingen 1634: 12,000-14,000 casualties of about 26,000 (46-54%), but most came in the rout after Horn ordered the withdrawal, so the share at withdrawal is lower and unknown (Nordlingen page). 0.3.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Light regimental guns grouped in batteries, shallow 5-6 rank infantry, and cavalry that 'could attack from the safety of an infantry line reinforced by cannon' (Gustavus Adolphus page; Roberts' Military Revolution thesis). Best in era.
weightNotes.initiative: Brigade system with capable subordinates (Horn, Baner, Torstensson, Bernhard); at Lutzen Bernhard kept attacking after the king fell (Lutzen page). Moderate.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The army in Germany lived by contributions, and supply failure drove it from Nuremberg: 'running short on provisions, Gustavus Adolphus was forced to withdraw' after the Alte Veste (Alte Veste page). Operations often outran supply.

summary: A national core of conscripted Swedish and Finnish infantry and cavalry, greatly expanded in Germany by mercenaries, organised in brigades fighting in shallow formations of 5-6 ranks with pike and musket. Light regimental guns accompanied the infantry and heavy artillery was massed in batteries; cavalry charged home with the sword, supported by detachments of musketeers. Gustavus led from the front, sought battle and drove his campaigns deep into the enemy's territory, feeding the army from contributions.
whyItWorked: Firepower and flexibility: shallow brigades, mobile guns and integrated cavalry out-shot and out-manoeuvred deep Imperial tercios at Breitenfeld (1631), where the Swedes re-formed a new front after their Saxon allies fled and broke Tilly's army. The Lech crossing at Rain (1632) under artillery and smoke killed Tilly. Roberts made this army the centre of his Military Revolution thesis (Military Revolution page), though the thesis is contested.
whereItFailed: Logistics and entrenchments: Wallenstein's fortified camp at the Alte Veste (1632) repulsed the assault and hunger forced a withdrawal. The system depended on the king: he was killed at Lutzen (1632), and at Nordlingen (1634) Horn and Bernhard attacked an entrenched Spanish-Imperial position, failed and lost the army in the retreat.

Guthrie, Battles of the Thirty Years War: From White Mountain to Nordlingen (Praeger, 2002)

name: US joint all-domain operations (2026)

weightNotes.aggression: FM 3-0 (2022) frames multidomain operations around seizing and retaining the initiative and converging effects offensively; 1991 and 2003 campaigns opened with the US attacking. Not 0.9: strategic posture since 2021 is deterrence first, and Iraq/Afghanistan made political leaders casualty- and commitment-averse.
weightNotes.maneuver: AirLand Battle heritage (FM 100-5 1982: initiative, depth, agility, synchronization) carried into FM 3-0; Desert Storm 1991 and the 2003 drive to Baghdad were manoeuvre campaigns that bypassed and dislocated rather than ground down.
weightNotes.flanking: The 1991 'left hook' through the western desert and 2003 bypass of Iraqi cities on the way to Baghdad show a doctrinal preference for envelopment over frontal attack.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Doctrine targets enemy forces and systems, not cities; urban fights (Fallujah 2004, Mosul 2016-17 by proxy) were accepted only when the enemy was there. Baghdad 2003 was taken by armoured raids, not siege.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Joint doctrine keeps a theatre reserve but the force-projection model commits most combat power early and relies on air/fires as the flexible reserve; low-middling.
weightNotes.scouting: Space, airborne ISR, SIGINT and organic drones at every echelon; RAND's Libya study shows even European air campaigns depended on US ISR. Highest of the modern profiles.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Units are pulled for reconstitution well before destruction and US political tolerance for casualties is low (Iraq 2003-11 narrative, AWC study), so formations disengage early; 0.2 kept below modern breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: FM 3-0 multidomain operations integrate land, air, maritime, space and cyber; joint fires and close air support are routine down to company level. The benchmark profile for this weight.
weightNotes.initiative: Mission command is codified doctrine (FM 3-0, ADP 6-0 lineage; FM 100-5 1982 already demanded initiative in subordinates); NCO corps and junior leaders trained to act on intent.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: The deepest expeditionary logistics system in the world, but operations do outrun it (the 2003 operational pause near Najaf after the sandstorm and fuel/ammo strain); strong but not absolute.

summary: A professional, expeditionary joint force that fights by first winning air and information superiority, then using precision fires from air, sea and land to strike enemy command, air defence and logistics in depth, and finally manoeuvring fast armoured and air-assault forces to dislocate and envelop rather than grind. FM 3-0 (2022) multidomain operations extend AirLand Battle to space and cyber, aimed at a peer adversary's integrated air defence and long-range fires. Carrier and amphibious forces give global reach.
whyItWorked: Against conventional opponents the combination of ISR dominance, precision strike and well-trained manoeuvre units has been decisive: Iraq 1991 collapsed in 100 hours of ground war and the 2003 invasion reached Baghdad in three weeks. Mission command and a professional NCO corps let small units exploit fleeting opportunities, and logistics allow sustained operations anywhere in the world.
whereItFailed: Conventional victory did not translate into political outcomes: Iraq 2003-2011 slid into insurgency and civil war after the invasion (US Army War College study, Vol. 1), and Afghanistan 2001-2021 ended with the collapse of the Afghan state the US had built. CSIS's 2023 Taiwan wargames suggest that against a peer with long-range strike the US would still win the first battle but lose dozens of ships and hundreds of aircraft, so the 1991-style asymmetry cannot be assumed.
