name: US Army and Navy doctrine (1941-1945)

weightNotes.aggression: Marshall's direct strategy: invade Europe and drive on Germany, island assaults across the Pacific; FM 100-5 (1941) is built round the offensive. Broad-front advance kept pressure everywhere.
weightNotes.maneuver: Mix: Cobra breakout and the Third Army pursuit across France (August 1944) were fast mobile operations; Lorraine, the Hurtgen Forest and Italy were grinding firepower attrition. Middle value.
weightNotes.flanking: Pacific 'leapfrogging' bypassed strongpoints (Rabaul, Truk); Falaise envelopment and Patton's Bulge relief turn. Many ETO attacks were frontal on a broad front.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Took ports and fortress cities when logistics demanded (Cherbourg, Brest, Aachen, Metz) but the target was the German army; low-moderate.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The broad-front policy left thin reserves: in December 1944 SHAEF's reserve was essentially two airborne divisions when the Ardennes offensive hit. Low.
weightNotes.scouting: Air reconnaissance, Ultra and Magic codebreaking (Midway was won on it) gave strong ISR; the Ardennes surprise of December 1944 shows its limit.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Units were kept in line and fed individual replacements rather than withdrawn; good-order withdrawals at moderate loss. Judgment.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Fire direction centres let one observer call in several artillery battalions, 'an unprecedented degree of infantry-artillery integration' (House ch. 3); tank-infantry teams, tactical air commands working with armies, and joint amphibious assault. Organization of Ground Combat Troops (CMH 2-1) on balanced divisions.
weightNotes.initiative: FM 100-5 (1941) warns that rigid rules 'limit imagination and initiative which are so important'; junior leaders improvised (hedgerow cutters in Normandy). Less systematic than German Auftragstaktik.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Unmatched supply organisation (Liberty ships, Red Ball Express), but the September 1944 pursuit outran supply and Third Army halted for fuel; Market Garden and the broad front competed for fuel. Fairly high.

summary: A mass army built almost from scratch on a standard 'triangular' division, fully motorised, backed by the largest industrial economy and a two-ocean navy. Doctrine (FM 100-5, 1941) stressed the offensive and combined arms; in practice the Army relied on firepower and material: artillery massed through fire direction centres, tank-infantry teams, fighter-bombers controlled by tactical air commands, and lavish logistics. In the Pacific the Navy and Marines fought a carrier and amphibious war, leapfrogging Japanese strongholds; the Army Air Forces ran daylight precision strategic bombing of Germany and the fire raids on Japan.
whyItWorked: Industrial output, motorisation and logistics let the US sustain offensives on two sides of the world at once. Artillery and air power compensated for average infantry tactical skill; after a steep learning curve (North Africa) the Army adapted quickly. Carrier aviation and codebreaking turned the Pacific war at Midway (June 1942), and amphibious technique matured from Guadalcanal and Tarawa to Normandy and Okinawa.
whereItFailed: Pearl Harbor and the Philippines 1941-42 (Bataan surrendered April 1942); Kasserine Pass, February 1943, where green troops with poor command arrangements were routed; Anzio 1944, which stalled on the beachhead; the Hurtgen Forest, September 1944 to February 1945, frontal attacks in terrain that cancelled US firepower and mobility; the Ardennes surprise of December 1944 against a thinly held broad front; costly assaults on fortified islands (Tarawa, Peleliu, Iwo Jima). The individual replacement system wore down infantry divisions kept in the line.

name: Zulu kingdom amabutho (1816-1879)

weightNotes.aggression: Every major battle of 1879 was a Zulu attack on a British position: Isandlwana, Rorke's Drift, Kambula, Gingindlovu, Ulundi (battle pages; Laband, Kingdom in Crisis). Not 1.0 because Cetshwayo's strategy was defensive, fighting only inside Zululand.
weightNotes.maneuver: Fast foot movement: the Undi Corps marched about 30 km and then stormed Rorke's Drift for some 11.5 hours; the main army of 20,000 approached Isandlwana unseen and lay concealed in the Ngwebeni valley (Rorke's Drift, Isandlwana pages). Tactics were assault, not manoeuvre, so 0.6.
weightNotes.flanking: The 'horns and chest of the buffalo' was the standard battle formation, aimed at encircling the enemy, and it closed round the British camp at Isandlwana (Isandlwana, Impi pages). Very high.
weightNotes.siegePreference: No siege capability: fortified positions were either stormed (Rorke's Drift, Kambula) or blockaded (Eshowe). Near zero.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The formation kept a reserve, the 'loins', behind the chest; at Isandlwana it was the uncommitted Undi Corps that went on to Rorke's Drift (Rorke's Drift page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: A screening force of mounted scouts and parties of 200-400 warriors kept the British from sighting the main columns before Isandlwana (Isandlwana page). Good for the era and means.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Gingindlovu 1879: 12,000 attackers left 1,100 dead and wounded before fleeing, about 9% (Gingindlovu page). Rorke's Drift 1879: 3,000-4,000 attackers lost at least 500 killed, about 12-17%, then withdrew by dawn (Rorke's Drift page). Kambula 1879: about 2,000 dead and wounded (official estimate) before breaking under mounted pursuit; impi size not given on the page. Isandlwana 1879: lost 1,000-3,000 of 20,000 (5-15%) and won (Isandlwana page). The break was usually a rout. 0.12.
weightNotes.combinedArms: A single arm: spear and shield infantry with some badly used firearms ('the arms of a coward', Rorke's Drift page); no cavalry, no artillery. Low.
weightNotes.initiative: Regimental izinduna commanded on the field, but control of the young regiments was loose: Buller's mounted troops 'stung' the Nkobamakosi on the right horn into a premature attack at Kambula (Kambula page). Moderate-low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Boys carried rations and cattle were driven as a moving larder (Impi page), which kept an impi in the field only days; after Isandlwana the army dispersed home (Laband). The army moved light and ignored supply lines: low.

summary: A citizen army organised by age-grade regiments (amabutho) quartered at royal homesteads, every adult man a soldier. Warriors fought on foot with the short stabbing spear (iklwa), throwing spears and a cowhide shield, in the 'horns and chest of the buffalo': the chest pinned the enemy, the horns ran round both flanks to encircle, and the loins waited in reserve. Armies moved fast and light behind a screen of scouts and attacked in mass. In 1879 they faced breech-loading rifles, artillery and Gatling guns.
whyItWorked: Against African neighbours the system was revolutionary: discipline, close-quarter weapons and encirclement built the kingdom under Shaka. Against a British force that dispersed in the open it was decisive: at Isandlwana (22 January 1879) 20,000 Zulus approached unseen, enveloped the camp and killed over 1,300 troops.
whereItFailed: Against concentrated breech-loader fire from a prepared position the mass assault could not close: Rorke's Drift (some 150 defenders held), Kambula (785 Zulu bodies counted near the camp), Gingindlovu and Ulundi (no warrior got within 30 yards of the square, Zulu power broken in half an hour). Earlier, Boer wagon laagers had done the same at Blood River (1838). Short logistics meant the army could not stay mobilised to wear down an invader.
